This title was previously used as an entry term for the hydration context. Later review only confirmed that it appeared in the `@platform` import group at the top of the file; the old wording should be understood as the search hypothesis at the time.

## Four groups of clues left at the top of the file

This record is based on the following visible excerpt:

```ts
import { globalScripts } from '@app-globals';
import { addHostEventListeners, getHostRef, loadModule, plt, registerHost, setScopedSSR } from '@platform';
import { connectedCallback, insertVdomAnnotations } from '@runtime';
import { CMP_FLAGS } from '@utils';
```

`globalScripts` was listed on its own under `@app-globals`. It was not grouped with listeners, host references, or runtime callbacks; there had also been no reason to draw it into the event branch. When checking this file, treating it first as a standalone import is closer to the original structure than putting all names at the top of the file into one hydration chain.

`@platform` was the group most emphasized in the old notes: `addHostEventListeners`, `getHostRef`, `loadModule`, `plt`, `registerHost`, and `setScopedSSR` were imported together. They show that the area adjacent to `hydrateApp` includes more than one listener name. The old diagram put `addHostEventListeners` first because its name points directly to a listener; `getHostRef` and `registerHost` are worth retaining as adjacent host-related search points. As for `loadModule`, `plt`, and `setScopedSSR`, this page does not record where they are used in function bodies, so their event order cannot be assigned based only on their being in the same import group.

The `connectedCallback` and `insertVdomAnnotations` under `@runtime` form another group. On the first read, these two names were placed in the "look later" category: they are adjacent to the hydration entry point, but the connection suggested by their names and the VDOM annotation should not replace checking where the listener leads. This separation remains useful, especially when the reading record retains only the file header and not the complete local context at the same time.

`CMP_FLAGS` is separate from `@utils`. Early records kept it outside the event path, and that has not changed. It may of course participate in a branch condition in this file, but no site showing it being read was retained here, so the flag check cannot be written up as established event behavior.

```text
hydrateApp
  ├─ @platform / addHostEventListeners
  ├─ @platform / getHostRef, registerHost
  ├─ @runtime / connectedCallback
  └─ @runtime / insertVdomAnnotations
```

The old notes also placed `globalScripts` outside the diagram. This choice is retained because it reminds readers that an import appearing in the same file does not mean every import participates in the same question. On later review, the platform group should apply the same restraint internally—`addHostEventListeners` is a priority lookup point, not a confirmed unique exit.

## Where to focus when reading the file

Start from the local reference to `hydrateApp`, and first highlight the statement where `addHostEventListeners` appears. If that is only a preparation or registration, continue following the object it receives; if it does not appear in the entry point's actual branch, the first arrow under the old title should stop there, and it should no longer be treated as the main line.

The point here is not to assign them responsibilities in advance, but to avoid conflating "event" and "host state" into the same process.

# R26.9 Import and Slot History

The compatibility train is provisionally tracking two issues side by side: which restrictions need to remain after style imports are expanded, and whether separate configuration metadata needs to be retained when a component uses manual slot assignment.

The initial working assumption was to "retain the information at compile time." That made it easier to include both issues in the same round, but was not enough to guide implementation. For style imports, the output is the style content that gets inserted; for slots, it is the result of a particular assignment. Both may appear to have produced output, but that output may no longer reveal the constraints it was originally subject to.

Three options were listed at the time.

1. After resolving the import target, retain only the expanded text and treat the modifiers as parse-time inputs.
2. During expansion, retain the restrictions attached to the import along with the style content, with the exact placement to be determined based on the style-processing path.
3. Use a shared auxiliary field for style conditions and slot state.

The third option is deferred. Style conditions constrain an imported style payload, while slot metadata describes component configuration. They are read at different times, and a shared field would force consumers to guess the context first. The first option should not be the default either: the presence of content does not mean the original restrictions are still in effect. Work on styles will provisionally follow the second option, but the order in which layer, function modifiers, and the following media are combined has not been settled.

For slots, we draw just one narrower distinction. A component with no slot and a component using manual slot assignment with no currently visible assignment should not be treated as the same state just because neither shows any content on the page. Information that identifies the configuration source needs to be retained; the field name, write location, and consumers have not been determined.

For the style-side review, start by tracing back from `src/compiler/style/css-imports.ts`. The file header includes `buildError`, `join`, `normalizePath`, the path module, declaration types, and `parseStyleDocs`. This shows that the area around import handling also involves paths and style document parsing; the filename alone is not enough to attribute every observed behavior to import semantics.

Decision for this round: styles and slots can be tracked in the same compatibility train, but will not share a single "generic metadata" solution. The style review needs to check whether the expanded content is still subject to the import conditions; the slot review needs to check whether a single empty assignment would erase the configuration source.

# R26.9 Import and Slot Evolution

The first draft grouped style imports and manual slot assignment under the phrase "information retained during the compilation phase." After review, that phrase can remain only as a starting point, not as a conclusion. Both involve state that later stages need to read, but the object the state is attached to, when it is meaningful, and how an incorrect result can overwrite it are different.

Retain the three initial candidate directions:

- When expanding an import, retain only the target stylesheet text; treat the modifiers, layer, and media as consumed input.
- When expanding, retain the constraints carried by the import so they continue to constrain the target stylesheet; actual style processing determines the final arrangement.
- Put style conditions and slot state into one piece of attached data without distinguishing their owning objects, and leave it to downstream code to interpret them by type.

The third did not carry into subsequent implementation discussions. On the surface, it reduces the number of objects passed around, but in practice it combines two values with different lifecycles: import conditions belong to the inlined style payload, while slot state comes from the allocation method used by the component. A field without explicit context forces the reader to guess its source from convention.

The first is particularly deceptive in the simplest samples. The target stylesheet can be found and can also appear in the output, so a reviewer may easily write "import processed." But this only shows that the text entered the expansion result; it does not show that the modifiers remain associated with that text. The second therefore remains the style-side direction, but the old draft's wording "retain conditions" is too broad. The functional modifiers on the import declaration, along with layer and subsequent media, need to be examined separately.

## Review Entry Point

The style investigation still starts at `src/compiler/style/css-imports.ts`. This location is the entry point left by the earlier investigation, and several adjacent responsibilities are visible here as well:

```ts
import { buildError, join, normalizePath } from '@utils'
import { basename, dirname, isAbsolute } from 'path'
import type * as d from '../../declarations'
import { parseStyleDocs } from '../docs/style-docs'
```

`join`, `normalizePath` and `isAbsolute` indicate that path assembly and absolute-path checks exist near import handling. When a sample cannot be expanded, first distinguish between the target not being found and the declaration being recognized but losing its conditions later. `buildError` also shows that this point is near an error branch; an error being reported does not replace checking the expansion result. `parseStyleDocs` appears at the head of the same file. It can only show that stylesheet document parsing is adjacent to this point; it cannot make the result of document parsing the semantic basis for the import declaration.

Therefore, this file is the starting point for the style-side investigation, not a reason to attribute the entire style chain to it. During review, first identify the sample's stage: path, declaration recognition, condition combination, or output payload. Earlier records collapsed these steps into "import has a problem," which later made it difficult to explain why samples that expanded successfully still behaved incorrectly.

## An Overly Broad Success Check

Existing records once classified imports with functional modifiers and imports with media as "parsing-compatible." This classification captures that both go through import processing, but misses what each still needs to express after expansion.

Functional modifiers are not merely hints used once while locating the target. If target content has already been inlined, the constraints they represent cannot disappear when lookup completes. Media is not merely a marker left after a successful import; it constrains the conditions under which the imported styles take effect. The two do not need to use the same textual form, but neither can be detached from the imported payload and left as an unowned result.

The review therefore separates the check into two questions. First, whether the declaration is recognized and obtains a target that can be expanded; second, whether, after the target content enters the expansion result, the constraints originally attached to it can still constrain that content. If the first succeeds and the second fails, it can no longer be recorded as "import passed."

## A Separate Decision for Slots

The slot question does not follow the style-side conclusion. The previous shortcut was: as long as no visible allocation is produced at that point, treat the component as having no slot. That is not sufficient.

A component having no slot at all means that the relevant capability is not part of the component's form. If a component uses manual slot assignment, the allocation method is part of its configuration; no visible allocation at a given moment cannot rewrite that configuration as nonexistent. The two cases may present the same empty result, but the empty result does not come from the same source.

Two recording methods were compared here: write a flag only when an allocation actually appears, or retain metadata from the component configuration for later identification. The latter was selected as the direction. The former would conflate an empty allocation with no slot and make the component's classification change with runtime timing. The latter's specific field name has not been decided, nor has the final read location been fixed to a particular layer; this round establishes only that the reader cannot use a single result to overwrite the configuration source.

## Review Addendum

During review, the original phrase "retain information uniformly" was split into narrower responsibilities:

| Object | What this round must confirm | What is not decided here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Style imports | Whether constraints still follow the style payload after expansion | The complete arrangement of conditions in the final output |
| Manual slot assignment | Whether metadata can distinguish the source of the component configuration | Field naming and every consumption point |

This table replaces the old wording "retain all metadata until the end." The latter did not identify who consumes the information or what observation could prove that the information had been lost.

## Retained Old Judgment

> As long as imported content reaches the output, the modifiers can be considered processed; a component with no allocation result can be treated as having no slot.

This passage is no longer the direction being followed. The first half conflates content being present with the constraints remaining effective; the second treats a runtime result as a component declaration. It is retained because regressions that inspect only expanded text or only an empty result may still follow these two assumptions.

The decision remains narrow: maintain style conditions and slot metadata separately, validating each against its own object. On the style side, continue tracing import replacement around `css-imports.ts`; on the slot side, continue checking the configuration source for manual slot assignment. Do not fold them back into a semantically ambiguous field just because they are part of the same round of compatibility work.

# R26.9 Imports and Slot Evolution

This record preserves two strands of history from a compatibility train. The style import issue was initially described as "can it be expanded?", while the slot issue was initially described as "is anything allocated?". Only later did it gradually become clear that both descriptions mistook a visible result in a process for the object itself.

They did not share an implementation object, nor should they share a universal state. The imported style payload needs to maintain its relationship with the import restrictions; the component's allocation method needs to maintain its relationship with the configuration source. The two strands were once tied together because both were called "metadata". The split is preserved below in the order in which the material was left behind.

## 2023-05-24: The Earliest Parallel Record

When it first entered the compatibility train, the style side recorded only one question: after `@import` was expanded, did the content attached to the declaration still need to be retained? The slot side recorded: did manual slot assignment need to leave a marker that later stages could recognize?

The shared working assumption at the time was "leave enough information during compilation". This had one practical benefit: it did not immediately require building a separate pipeline for each of the two topics, and it avoided naming fields before the implementation had been fully understood. It also had an obvious gap: it did not make clear who the information belonged to, when it would be read, or what result could prove that the information had been lost.

Three candidate directions were listed at the time.

1. For style imports, retain only the target text. Once path resolution is complete, the function modifiers, layer, and media are all treated as consumed input; on the slot side, look only at whether an actual assignment occurs.
2. For style imports, retain the restrictions carried by the declaration so that they continue to remain related to the imported content; on the slot side, retain identifiable source information from the component configuration.
3. Use one shared attached field for both sides. Style processing and component processing write their respective states into it, and later stages interpret it according to the object type.

The first option was not unreasonable at the time. The simplest import samples cared only whether the target could be found and whether the corresponding text could be seen in the output after expansion; the simplest component samples likewise cared only whether content had been assigned on the page. Using visible results as the criterion quickly produced a "success" or "failure". The problem was that this kind of success could answer only whether the result appeared, not whether it still carried the constraints that produced the result.

The third option was shelved early on. Import restrictions apply to a style payload, while slot information applies to the allocation method adopted by a component. Even if both were passed as some kind of structured value, their lifecycles and reading contexts were different. If they shared one field that was not tied to an object, the reader would first have to determine what the field represented at that moment before it could determine whether the value was correct; this uncertainty was harder to investigate than having one more piece of local data.

The second option was retained as the working direction, but it was not yet written as a complete requirement. The style side knew only that it could not discard all declaration content as plain text, while the slot side knew only that an empty assignment should not automatically equal no slot. There was still no conclusion about how to combine the conditions, how to name the metadata, or who the actual consumers were.

## 2023-05-25: Narrowing the scope in the early review

The early review did not produce a unified design diagram, but instead first rejected an incorrect way of organizing the concerns: do not let style conditions serve as evidence for slot state.

A brief statement from the review was recorded:

> First ask separately about the object and the reader. When style content appears, that does not establish how the component is configured; when a component is temporarily empty, that also does not prove that the import conditions have been handled.

The value of this addendum lay in changing the order of rechecking. Previously, both topics were broadly covered by "whether the information is still there", making it easy for reviewers to perform only a single snapshot comparison. After the review, the style side began treating "the import declaration is recognized" and "the expanded payload is still constrained" as two separate matters; the slot side began treating "no visible assignment has been produced" and "the component does not have a slot structure" as situations with different causes.

The review also evaluated a seemingly lighter-weight compromise: the style side would pass a boolean indicating whether the import had any additional modifiers, and the slot side would pass a boolean indicating whether the component had any special assignment. This compromise was not adopted. Booleans flattened the most important distinctions too early. The import side might need to handle the function-based modifier portion, layer and subsequent media at the same time; the slot side needed to distinguish no slot from manual slot assignment. If these were first reduced to "a special case exists" or "no special case exists", there would not be enough object relationships for later layers to reconstruct.

This review did not specify any particular field name, nor did it specify that all the logic should be placed in the same layer. It only established this: no subsequent approach could rely on a generic marker whose ownership could not be explained.

## Summer of 2023: The starting point for tracing style issues was established

Investigations into style issues later consistently started at `src/compiler/style/css-imports.ts`. This location was chosen because it was the entry point where the earlier investigation had left off, and because the top of the file already showed several adjacent responsibilities that were easy to conflate:

```ts
import { buildError, join, normalizePath } from '@utils'
import { basename, dirname, isAbsolute } from 'path'
import type * as d from '../../declarations'
import { parseStyleDocs } from '../docs/style-docs'
```

This code did not tell us that this file was responsible for the entire style-processing pipeline, but it was enough to help separate several phenomena.

`join`,`normalizePath` and `isAbsolute` show that this code is close to path construction and path checks. When an import sample cannot reach the target file, the state at the path level must be checked first; at that point it is too early to discuss whether the conditions are preserved after inlining.`buildError` indicates that error branches are also nearby, so "there is an error" likewise does not prove that a particular combination of conditions has been handled correctly.`parseStyleDocs` is among the direct dependencies, reminding reviewers not to conflate parsing the style document and handling import declarations into a single operation.`d` comes from declaration types, showing that this code works with structured objects, so not every phenomenon can be explained solely in terms of string replacement.

This entry established a fairly practical troubleshooting order: first ask whether the target can be located; then whether the import declaration is recognized; only after that ask whether the condition and payload after expansion are still related. Older records used to collapse these steps into "import failure," putting path issues, declaration issues, and semantic issues into a single conclusion. When successful samples were reviewed later, it was often possible only to confirm that the target text appeared, without knowing which step had previously been skipped.

## 2023-09-25: A single review that checked only for text

This round of review left behind a misjudgment that later became highly representative. The target style in the sample could be found, and the expanded text also appeared in the result, so the record said "the modifier portion had already been processed." There was a basis for that judgment at the time: examining the output text could indeed confirm that the import had not broken at the path, and could also confirm that the target content had been pulled in.

But its scope was too narrow. An import with a function modifier is not merely a lookup hint; once the target content is inlined, the constraint represented by the modifier still cannot disappear just because lookup has completed. media is not an incidental note attached after a successful import either; it specifies the conditions under which that imported style takes effect. Treating both as "details after successful parsing" would make the phenomenon of output containing text while no longer retaining the original relationship impossible to name.

Accordingly, later reviews no longer asked only, "Was anything expanded?" They were divided into two consecutive questions:

- whether the import declaration recognized a target that could be expanded;
- after the imported content entered the expansion result, whether the restrictions originally specified by the declaration still constrained that content.

Passing the first question cannot substitute for the second. Even when the target text is already present, the second question may still have failed; this is not an additional unrelated regression, but a semantic layer originally obscured by the four-character phrase "import succeeded."

This shift also explains why path checking must be performed independently first. If the target cannot be located, the conditional relationship has not yet begun to form; if the target has already been located and expanded, path correctness can no longer be used to mask whether the condition has become detached from the payload. Path tools near the file header make this separation easier to apply, but the separation itself comes from the different questions the samples answer.

## 2023-09-25: The retained old approach

The following old approach was once considered sufficient; its original meaning is retained here:

> During expansion, first pull in the target text; if media appears at the end of the declaration, append media once at the end of the output. The function modifier only affects whether expansion is possible. Leave layer for a later stage to handle uniformly.

This passage is now deprecated. It treats several restrictions as suffixes that can be appended at any position, and also assumes that restrictions and payload will naturally remain adjacent after expansion. What actually needs to be preserved is the relationship between objects, not a piece of text merely happening to appear at the end of the output.

"The function modifier only affects whether expansion is possible" is the old approach's most critical error. It treats successfully obtaining the target as evidence that the semantics have already been exhausted. The target can be obtained successfully, while the restriction may still not have followed the payload. Appending media separately at the end has the same problem: media must continue to constrain that imported style, rather than becoming an isolated marker detached from the object.

The statement "leave layer for unified handling in later stages" is retained here to show that, at the time, where it would be represented had not yet been decided, not to suggest that layer could be ignored. The context behind the old approach is still recognizable: the team wanted to handle path resolution, text inclusion, and final style arrangement separately first. Its failure was not in splitting the work into stages, but in failing to carry forward the relationships that needed to remain bound together when doing so.

This passage does not need to be deleted from the historical record. Regression tests that look only at output text could still reproduce the same line of thinking; keeping the original sentence makes it easier to identify where the misjudgment came from than sanitizing it into an abstract lesson.

## The slot workstream did not borrow conclusions from the style workstream

Early on, the discussion of manual slot assignment was overshadowed by style issues, because both were called "metadata". When reviewed separately later, what the slot side really needed to protect was not the result of any particular run, but the component's configuration source.

If a component has no slot, that form of the component does not include the relevant assignment capability. When a component uses manual slot assignment, the assignment mode is part of the component configuration, and even if no visible assignment has been established at a particular point in time, that configuration cannot be reclassified as "no slot". The two states may produce the same page appearance, but not for the same reason.

Two implementation approaches were compared on the slot side.

The first was to leave a marker only when an assignment actually occurred. This seemed simple to implement, and the runtime results were straightforward. Its problem was that an empty assignment would erase the distinction in source: both a component with no slot and a component using manual assignment that was currently empty would end up with no marker.

The second was to retain metadata from the component configuration for later stages to read, without letting runtime assignment results overwrite that source. This direction was chosen. It did not require every stage to copy the same field, nor did it lock down the final read point once and for all at the time; the decision was that the configuration source must remain distinguishable and must not be replaced by a single empty result.

The only thing this decision has in common with the style-side decision is that both reject replacing the source with visible results. They do not share a data structure. The style side concerns the relationship between import conditions and the imported style payload; the slot side concerns the relationship between component configuration and current assignment results. Grouping both sides back into the same kind of "special state" would return to the early mistake of using a shared field.

## Correction record for the old conclusion

The old draft contained this summary:

> As long as the imported content reaches the output, the modifiers can be considered handled; components with no assignment results can be treated as having no slot.

This summary no longer applies and is retained near its original location as the source for the correction.

The problem with the first half is that it conflates "content has been included" with "the conditions remain in effect". Seeing the target styles in the expanded result only shows that the content made it into the result for that sample; it does not prove that function modifiers, layer, or media still constrain those styles.

The problem with the second half is that it treats the runtime result at a single point in time as a component declaration. The absence of assignment results may mean that there was no visible content at the time, or that the component uses manual assignment but has not yet produced a result; it does not imply that the component has no slot, much less justify deleting the configuration source.

After this correction, this page no longer uses "metadata retention" as an umbrella term for both topics. The style side only discusses whether the conditions remain with the payload; the slot side only discusses whether the configuration source remains identifiable. Their appearance in the same compatibility train does not mean they should be carried by the same object.

## Addendum to the 2024 meeting notes: Counterexamples are more useful than snapshots of success

The later meeting addendum did not require compiling all possible combinations into one large table, but instead required a clear explanation of two types of counterexamples.

The first type of counterexample is: the target styles already appear in the expanded output, but the restrictions on the import declaration can no longer apply to them. These examples refute the old assumption that "seeing the text means the work is done". They do not need to prove that every output layout is wrong, only to point out that the presence of content cannot replace conditional relationships.

The second type of counterexample is: a component currently has no visible assignments, so it is classified as having no slot; only when the component configuration is examined later does it become clear that it uses manual slot assignment. These examples refute the old assumption that "an empty result means there is no slot". Likewise, they do not require inventing a new set of markers for every component form, only ensuring that a temporary result cannot override the source.

The meeting also confirmed that the two counterexamples would be maintained separately. The style example cannot validate slot state, and the slot example cannot be used to infer import conditions. Previously, because they were both in the same batch of the compatibility train, the review table had shown a tendency to record "both examples succeeded" as an overall pass; this wording was not retained. The two examples answer questions about different objects.

Regarding the style entry point, the meeting addendum continued the existing layered approach: when the target file has not been located, handle path and declaration recognition first; when the target has already been expanded, then check whether the conditions and payload are still paired. This does not treat `css-imports.ts` as the sole point of responsibility, but instead prevents success at an earlier layer from masking what is missing at a later layer.

## Adjacent Issues Not Yet Separated Out

One adjacent issue on the style side has still not been settled on this page: where the conditions on an import declaration are ultimately incorporated into the output. The current material is sufficient to show that certain relationships must not be lost, but not enough to assign fixed implementation responsibility for where all combinations of conditions are expressed. In particular, the fact that `css-imports.ts` contains path utilities, types, and style document parsing does not justify assigning the subsequent stages to this file as well.

The slot side also retains an open question: once the configuration source is preserved, which paths only read that source, and which paths also take the current assignment results into account. This question will affect where subsequent follow-up checks should resume, but it does not change the distinction already made: an empty assignment cannot reclassify manual slot assignment as no slot.

The two unresolved issues will no longer be combined into follow-up work on "compatibility metadata". The former concerns import expansion and its style payload, while the latter concerns component configuration and the slot lifecycle. Keeping two entry points is more useful than creating a seemingly unified to-do item that cannot explain the boundaries between objects.

## Current Decision

At this point, the early assumptions that "successful expansion is enough" and "an empty result is enough for classification" are both no longer valid. The current requirement on the style side is: when `replaceImportDeclarations` inlines `@import` with a function modifier, it must preserve the layer semantics, subsequent media conditions, and imported style payload together.

This requirement supersedes the old direction of plain-text expansion. It does not require proving the implementation correct through any one fixed text layout, nor does it require putting style conditions and slot information into a temporary structure; it requires that, after inlining, the layer semantics, subsequent media conditions, and imported style payload must not become detached from one another.

The narrower decision is retained on the slot side: manual slot assignment as a source of component configuration must be distinguishable in subsequent checks, and cannot be replaced by the outcome of a single case with no visible assignment. The specific field name and full read path are still left to the adjacent issues, and are not arbitrarily fixed here.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> import_declaration
    state "Import declaration" as import_declaration
    state "Path handling" as path_handling
    state "Style payload expansion" as style_expansion
    state "Conditions retained with the payload" as condition_preserved
    state "Manual assignment configuration" as manual_assignment
    state "Component Metadata" as component_metadata
    import_declaration --> path_handling
    path_handling --> style_expansion
    style_expansion --> condition_preserved
    condition_preserved --> [*]
    manual_assignment --> component_metadata
    component_metadata --> [*]
```

The two endpoints in the diagram do not indicate that they share the same implementation. The upper half only shows that after an import declaration goes through path handling and payload expansion, the conditions still need to remain with the payload; the lower half only shows that the manual assignment configuration needs to leave a recognizable Component Metadata. The diagram retains two branches precisely to avoid folding them back into the earlier idea of a shared field.

## Legacy Examples Appendix

### Legacy example: Only checking the expanded text

The legacy example's check consisted of providing a parseable `@import`, confirming that the target style text appeared in the expanded result, and stopping there. This example can still help identify cases where the target cannot be found, path checks behave abnormally or the import declaration has not been processed at all. But it can no longer serve as evidence of semantic correctness when a function modifier or trailing media is present, because it does not check whether the conditions still constrain the imported style payload.

### Legacy example: Empty assignment means no slot

The check in the earlier example observes a single runtime result, and classifies the component as having no slot if no visible assignment is shown. It may happen to reach the correct conclusion for components that truly have no slot, but it cannot distinguish component structure from a transient result. For manual slot assignment, this check would erase the configuration source that should be preserved.

### Earlier example: Shared auxiliary fields

An early draft envisioned sharing auxiliary fields between style conditions and slot state. That proposal did not become part of the current direction. It is retained not to reopen the discussion of field reuse, but to explain why the two topics still cannot be combined even when both are called "metadata": reusing fields does not reduce semantic differences, it only defers object identification to a later reader.

The earlier examples in this record can continue to help identify entry points for historical regressions, but they cannot override the current decision. On the style side, trace back from import expansion and payload relationships; on the slot side, trace back from component configuration and manual slot assignment Metadata. The two tracks meet in the same compatibility train, but at this point they still maintain their respective decision boundaries.

# sourcemap return shape design

The compatibility check in R26.9 conflates chunks that have no sourcemap with those that "have a map, but its contents are empty." Keeping the returned record in object form seems like it could eliminate a caller-side branch; the initial draft therefore leans toward supplying an empty object when there is no map and letting later stages inspect its contents.

This is just a candidate approach, not an interface decision. An empty object would prevent consumers from distinguishing "no mappings were generated in this run" from "mappings were generated but had no sourcesContent." These two states look similar in the logs but mean different things.

We're comparing three return shapes:

- Keep a null value when map is missing;
- Supply an empty object when map is missing to keep the record's fields stable;
- Skip the record outright in an earlier branch.

The second option is the least work for callers that read the fields, but it disguises the missing state as a readable mapping object. The third changes the number of records and makes it harder during debugging to tell whether the chunk was included in the output.

Another issue we haven't yet broken out is dev-only source map. We can't decide on it solely on the basis that "development environments need debugging," because we first need to establish what a chunk without a sourcemap should leave behind. Once the return shape and generation conditions have been separated, we'll decide whether the dev-only path needs a separate trial.

# sourcemap return shape design

The initial draft put too much weight on "keeping the field shape stable." That reasoning has been retained after review because it explains why someone might argue for filling in an empty object, but it isn't enough to decide the interface. A chunk without a sourcemap is not the same as an empty sourcemap: the latter still indicates that generation took place.

This review was limited to the entry point left by `src/utils/sourcemaps.ts`. There are two type dependencies at the top of the file:

```ts
import type { SourceMap as RollupSourceMap } from 'rollup';
import type * as d from '../declarations';
```

They show that this code touches both Rollup's mapping types and the record types in the local declarations. The type names themselves don't say what a missing map should be converted to, nor do they support "creating a mapping just to make the field exist." Previously, treating an empty object as a safe default mistook convenience at the declaration layer for output semantics.

## Options retained after review

**Preserve the missing value.** Callers need to check `map`, at the cost of an extra branch; the benefit is that the output record can still express that the chunk has no sourcemap. This option doesn't flatten the original state.

**Fill in an empty object.** The old draft favored this option because consuming code could go straight into the map-handling path. It now appears to create an intermediate state that's hard to explain: the object exists, but it wasn't produced by sourcemap generation. In particular, an object containing only an empty sourcesContent can easily be treated in downstream processing as a valid but incomplete mapping.

**Drop the record.** This avoids the null check on `map`, but turns "the chunk exists and has no mapping" into "there is no output record for it." If an investigation is focused on output counts, this change is harder to trace than a null value.

The recommendation is therefore to trial the first option, stop treating the second as the default recommendation, and discuss the third only if the record itself serves no other purpose. This recommendation remains limited to returned records; it has not been extended into a rule for handling all build artifacts.

## Where dev-only fits

dev-only source map is still a separate decision point. It concerns when to generate one, while the return shape addresses how to represent a missing generation result. If both change together, any difference will be impossible to attribute to either the condition switch or the return-value conversion. The trial should first fix the representation of a missing map, then check whether development conditions lead to additional mapping records.

The rollback conditions are narrowed accordingly: if preserving the missing value prevents existing consumers from distinguishing normal chunks from anomalous records, or if processing can only continue by fabricating a map, stop the trial, return to the record consumers, and rework the separation of paths that need a map. Do not restore the empty-object approach just to maintain the object's shape.

# sourcemap return shape design

This record is still used to explain the earlier interface disagreement over R26.9, so the original section on "filling in an empty object" has not been removed. That approach is no longer recommended, but it left a useful reminder: a consumer's desire for stable fields is a separate question from whether the output should claim that a sourcemap exists.

The initial question wasn't whether the map's contents were complete, but how to pass the record downstream after a chunk with no sourcemap had already reached output processing. The first draft focused on object shape, assuming that callers would need fewer branches as long as `map` could always be read. This overlooked a more practical counterexample: an object created as a placeholder would suggest that the mapping generation stage had left behind some result, when in fact the chunk never had a sourcemap.

## Archived earlier proposal

The earlier proposal was to fill in missing values with an empty object, treating an empty `sourcesContent` as a harmless placeholder. The benefit was straightforward: consumers wouldn't have to check whether `map` existed first, and the access path would be cleaner at the type level. At the time, this was seen as a way to reduce compatibility costs.

During a later review, the discussion shifted from "can the field be read?" to "what does this object represent?" A map with empty contents is still a mapping object; if there is no map, there is no corresponding mapping object. Collapsing the two into the same shape would make it impossible to tell which case applied from the record itself when investigating output. The earlier proposal is retained here to explain the trade-off at the time and should no longer be used as a basis for implementation.

Another approach that had been proposed was to omit the record entirely. That would avoid an empty value but also erase any indication of whether the chunk had appeared at all. For consumers concerned only with map files, this looked clean; for those needing to check the output set, the change in record count would instead add ambiguity. This approach was not included in the trial scope.

## Boundaries indicated by the file entry point

This page still points to `src/utils/sourcemaps.ts`. The only dependencies visible at the top of the file are Rollup's `SourceMap` type and the type namespace from the local `../declarations`:

```ts
import type { SourceMap as RollupSourceMap } from 'rollup';
import type * as d from '../declarations';
```

Here, `RollupSourceMap` identifies the external mapping type, while `d` connects the returned record to the local declarations. Neither is enough to automatically interpret a missing value as an empty map. Someone had taken "the local record needs a field" to mean "the field must hold an object"; that interpretation was withdrawn in this review. A record can have a `map` field, but the field's value must still reflect whether a map was generated.

This also limits what this page can resolve: it discusses how maps are represented in output records, not whether Rollup should generate sourcemaps, and certainly does not treat the way types are declared as a build condition. Once these layers were separated, the empty-object proposal lost its main original rationale.

## Current return semantics

Within that scope, the later correction was explicit:

> When `generateRollupOutput` processes a Rollup chunk with no sourcemap, the returned record's `map` must be undefined, not a synthesized object containing only an empty sourcesContent.

This correction addresses only the no-sourcemap input case. It does not require the contents of any existing map to be rewritten, nor does it classify a real map with an empty sourcesContent as missing. The decision should start with whether the chunk has a sourcemap and use that to determine the record's `map`; it must not work backwards by filling in a value for caller convenience.

Keeping `undefined` means consumers must account for a branch: process the map when one exists, and still retain the chunk's other output information when no map exists. This branch is part of the interface semantics, not a temporary compatibility patch. If a consumer accepts only objects, the consumer side should explain why it handles only records with maps, rather than fabricating nonexistent maps during output processing.

## The dev-only discussion was not resolved by this

The old title grouped dev-only source map with this issue because the two came up together at the time, not because they should be handled by the same switch. dev-only determines under which build conditions maps are generated; the return semantics here determine how the record expresses that no map was generated. A change to the former could change the number of chunks with maps; the latter should not disguise that change as maps with empty contents.

This page therefore records just the trial order: first check chunks without sourcemaps against the missing-value semantics, then separately observe whether maps are actually generated under development conditions. If the two changes are bundled into one submission and differences appear, it will be impossible to tell whether they came from the generation conditions or the return conversion. This order is intended to narrow the investigation; it does not mean a general rule has been chosen for dev-only source map.

## Rollback and unresolved points

If a consumer is later found to fail because `map` is `undefined`, first confirm whether it actually needs a sourcemap; do not simply restore the empty object. Only when that consumer's input contract explicitly requires a valid mapping object should filtering or adjustments be made at its own boundary. The output record should still accurately preserve the missing state.

This proposal once treated "no map" and "an empty sourcesContent" as the same compatibility issue; that has been corrected, but the exact scope of the dev-only condition has not been settled here. That part still needs to be assessed separately against the actual generation conditions.

# Migration guide for media nesting and cross-document styles

## The old entry point is still usable, but no longer serves as evidence for both behaviors

This round of follow-up notes starts by correcting a shortcut in the initial draft: pseudo-class nesting inside media and Cross-document Constructable Stylesheets should not be described as following the same path by default. Both are in scope for the compatibility train review, and readers can reach this page from the same issue record; this only means they need to be checked side by side, not that the same code handles them.

The known test location in the repository remains:

`src/compiler/style/css-parser/test/parse-serialize.spec.ts`

The direct connections visible at the top of the file have not changed:

```ts
import { parseCss } from '../parse-css';
import { serializeCss } from '../serialize-css';
```

These two imports have a specific use in the migration: when you have CSS text, you can preserve the input on the test side, then record parsing and serialization observations separately. They do not show where the constructable stylesheet is created, or whether the other document consumes the raw text or an already-processed style payload.

## The combined path in the initial draft

The old draft suggested putting the two examples in this order: take the media snippet, pass it through `parseCss`, then hand it to `serializeCss`, and finally compare the cross-document page results. This sequence looked convenient for migrating both at once because only one example would need to be maintained; review showed that it had bundled multiple gaps into a single sentence.

The first gap is in the media example itself. The test file can serve as a starting point for tracing the issue, but the old record retained neither the failing text nor enough material to distinguish a "change during parsing" from a "change during serialization." Even if the page shows a different result, that result does not establish which step introduced the change.

The second gap is on the cross-document consumer side. The old record has no caller name, actual version, or construction entry point. Without those details, there is no way to know whether it receives the same style text, much less use it as downstream validation of the serializer.

So this combined path is kept on record, but is no longer used as a migration procedure. Restoring the old example means restoring the CSS input and test entry point, not the assumption that "the two issues must follow the same path."

## Identify what you have before migrating

When you pick this up later, first identify which kind of material you have:

- Raw CSS text, which can be used for a local comparison in parser/serializer;
- Already-generated output text, which needs to be marked as not being the original input;
- An already-constructed stylesheet object, for which the only starting point is its caller;
- If all that remains is page behavior, with no input or entry point, do not turn it into a test case yet.

The point of this distinction is not tidier categorization, but avoiding a comparison that only looks stable because result text was pasted back in as input. If the input has already been minified, concatenated, or serialized elsewhere, what the tests see is no longer the same as what was present in the user's environment; save it as candidate output rather than using it to replace the original example.

The migration starting point for the media branch is still the original style snippet. When placing the snippet in `parse-serialize.spec.ts`, preserve the media block and the pseudo-class selectors inside it; do not expand the selectors further to fit the test format. Then record both ends: the nesting visible after parsing, and the CSS text produced by serialization. If either end is missing, all that can be said is that the example has been placed near the tests, not that the issue has been pinpointed.

The cross-document branch does not start from the file above. First find a caller that still uses constructable stylesheets, then check the actual version, entry point, and current result. Check the two branches in the same round only if material from the caller shows that the style payload it uses is indeed comparable to the media example; otherwise, just preserve the originals for each branch.

## Practical reminders in the margin

During one review, someone used "the test filename contains parse-serialize" as a basis for attributing the issue. That judgment was later crossed out. The filename and imports only show local relationships on the test side; the cross-document issue still needs its own entry point. Similar visual results cannot fill that gap either.

If a new example has no output text to compare, stop at the input source. Do not use whether the page looks fixed to fill the gap between parse and serialize. If all you have is a cross-document case, stop at locating the caller; do not work backward and change parser tests to manufacture an unconfirmed link.

To restore the old path, you can follow these steps:

```text
Original CSS snippet
  -> Put it back in the original test location
  -> Preserve the original media and pseudo-class structure
  -> Recheck the parsing side and the serialization side

Cross-document case
  -> Return to the known caller
  -> Reconfirm the version and entry point
```

Here, "put it back" means only restoring the example used for comparison, not automatically reinstating a particular fix. No file-level restore point can be specified for the cross-document branch until a caller is identified.

## Remaining gaps

There is still no single piece of material that establishes at which stage the nesting inside media changes, and none showing that Cross-document Constructable Stylesheets uses the same serialized output. The old record points from the issue name and call name to this test file; the actual relationship still needs to be checked against the references from that time.

TODO:

- Add the original input and corresponding output text for the media example.
- Record where the parsing observations and serialization observations were each made.
- Find a caller that still uses Cross-document Constructable Stylesheets.
- Record the actual version, entry point, and current result at that caller.

Until these gaps are filled, this page can be used to migrate the old CSS example back to the test entry point and to remind whoever takes over not to merge the two review tracks; it cannot establish where responsibility lies for constructable stylesheets.

# Migration Guide for media Nesting and Cross-Document Styles

This page has always been filed under R26.9 Compatibility Train, with pseudo-class nesting inside media and Cross-document Constructable Stylesheets listed side by side in its title. That pairing remains in place today: it makes both types of examples easy to find from the compatibility-check entry point, and preserves how the original cases were grouped. What has been dropped over the past few years is the practice of misreading that pairing as a single implementation chain.

The earliest traceable file location has not changed:

`src/compiler/style/css-parser/test/parse-serialize.spec.ts`

The direct dependency recorded at the top of that file is:

```ts
import { parseCss } from '../parse-css';
import { serializeCss } from '../serialize-css';
```

This page has accumulated several layers of notes from different points in time around this entry point. Some sections are useful only for restoring old examples, while others have already been disproved by later counterexamples. When migrating, do not skip the old sections and simply extract a conclusion; first confirm whether the material you have is CSS text or an actual cross-document case involving constructed stylesheets.

## 2023-06: First preserve a reproducible CSS

The first version had only a very narrow goal. When someone brings in pseudo-class nesting inside a media block, do not start by simplifying the selector, and do not remove media just to fit it into a test. The original snippet itself is the basis for comparison; once the nesting is expanded or split up beforehand, it is no longer possible to tell whether the test rewrote the input or the processing changed the meaning of the styles.

The actionable steps at the time were: place an independently reproducible CSS snippet near `parse-serialize.spec.ts`, preserve the input, and examine parsing and serialization separately. The early records did not preserve a complete call graph, nor did they attempt to infer runtime responsibilities from this file. It was only a local test entry point.

During the same period, Cross-document Constructable Stylesheets was noted only as a separate issue thread. The old notes did not include where the document was created, where the stylesheet was used, or the caller's version. The approach at the time was to leave it aside and wait for someone to bring back the actual entry point, rather than fill in the gaps with the test file's path.

This early rule remained useful later on: when restoring a media example, first restore the original CSS and the original test location. But it was never sufficient for migrating cross-document cases.

## A side note left beside the tests

A very brief reminder was once left near the test entry point: do not take the filename "parse-serialize" as an indication of issue ownership. This reminder was not elaborated on at first, but it still held up under later review.

The reason is specific. The import at the top of the file only confirms that the test file directly uses `parseCss` and `serializeCss`. It does not tell us that all styles enter through this entry point, nor does it tell us whether the constructable stylesheet in another document receives the original CSS, processed text, or a payload from elsewhere. Treating the filename as a boundary of responsibility can cause a cross-document branch to be incorrectly forced into parser tests without a caller.

Therefore, when you encounter the two types of material, separate them first:

- If the original CSS can be provided, treat it as a media sample;
- If only the result of a constructable stylesheet can be provided, treat it as a caller-side scenario;
- If text is already output from somewhere, first mark it as an output candidate, and do not relabel it as parser input;
- If the material only describes differences on the page and has no input or entry point, retain the observed behavior, and do not force it into a test case.

This is not an abstract classification. It determines whether a sample can be reconstructed. If output text is mistaken for input, the comparison only yields a result that has been processed a second time; if observed page behavior is mistaken for a parser failure, it also obscures the gap in how the stylesheet is created and used.

## An earlier attempt to merge them into a single migration chain

A later draft arranged the two issues into a short workflow: first pass the media fragment to `parseCss`, then to `serializeCss`, and finally use the cross-document result for comparison. The advantage of writing it this way was that only one sample needed to be maintained; this also made its problems harder to see.

This approach implicitly relied on two unproven assumptions.

First, the user scenario involving pseudo-class nesting inside media actually passes through the two functions seen in the test file. The imports on the test side make this worth checking, but they cannot replace a comparison of the actual inputs and outputs.

Second, Cross-document Constructable Stylesheets's caller obtains the same serialized result. The old records contain no caller version, no creation entry point, and no usage location, so there is no way to determine whether this assumption holds.

There was also a third practical problem: the draft did not preserve the failing text. Even if differences in the styling results were observed at the time, people looking at it later would have no way of knowing whether the change occurred during parse, during serialize, or after the stylesheet was moved to another document. Similar-looking pages cannot substitute for two text snippets or object entry points.

This merged approach was not adopted as a migration step. It is retained because someone from the early days may still find this page using the old keyword "unify serialization first"; it no longer applies. When restoring the old path, restore only the original CSS fragment and the test entry point, not the assumption that "both observed behaviors must follow the same path".

## 2024-06: Split sample migration into two tracks

The next addendum did not replace the test file, but changed the migration order. First determine the type of material, then decide where to put it.

### media samples

For the original CSS text, keep the following order:

1. Preserve the original snippets from the user's environment, without preprocessing either the media blocks or the pseudo-class hierarchy.
2. Move independently comparable snippets to the matching test locations in `src/compiler/style/css-parser/test/parse-serialize.spec.ts`.
3. Record the structure seen on the parser side separately from the text produced on the serializer side.
4. When the output differs from the input, preserve both texts; when there is no output, make clear whether processing stopped at the input, parsing, or serialization stage.
5. If a rollback is needed, revert the newly added examples or restore the original examples, without making incidental changes to cross-document callers.

"Record separately" is especially important here. The original input documents the user's situation; the parsed content is used to determine whether the nesting relationships have been preserved; the serialized text is used to assess the output form. Collapsing all three into "the styles are fine" loses the most useful information about where the differences are.

### Cross-document examples

For constructable stylesheets, the order is reversed: first find the callers that are still using them, then verify the actual version, entry point, and current result. Without this information, you cannot infer the creation path from the CSS tests, nor can you describe it as a direct consequence of `serializeCss`.

Once the caller is confirmed, you must still first establish what it holds: the original CSS, serialized text, or an already-constructed stylesheet object. Only once this is clear is there a basis for including it in the same comparison as the style payload in the media branch. If they do not use the same type of material, preserve each case separately, and do not invent a seemingly unified fix path.

The previous version listed "find the caller" as a one-line to-do, which could easily be misread as meaning that finding a name was enough. What actually needs to be recorded is three things: the caller's actual version, the point where it enters the constructable stylesheet path, and the current result. If any one of these is missing, the cross-document results should not be equated with the output of parser/serializer.

## Review addendum: Similar results do not mean a shared entry point

A review revised the old conclusion to a more conservative statement: the test file can serve as a checkpoint for media examples, but cannot by itself establish responsibility for cross-document examples.

This change affected the stopping points during migration. If you have reproducible CSS text, you can proceed down the testing branch, preserve the original text, and compare parsing and serialization. If all you have is a user's cross-document result, stop at locating the caller; do not write a parser test based on assumptions just to keep moving forward.

The review also retained a reminder in the form of a counterexample: both cases may show "styles do not match expectations", but this is only a symptom, not evidence that they share the same entry point. If they are merged based on their visual results, subsequent fixes might only make the test text look correct, while there would still be no identifiable place to investigate for cross-document usage.

This addendum did not invalidate the old test entry point. It requires asking one more question before using that entry point: are we now migrating the CSS example, or the caller's actual environment? The migration materials and recovery points differ depending on the answer.

## On-call addendum: recovery targets must not be conflated

In subsequent on-call work, a common mistake was to interpret "restore the old path" as reverting all changes associated with the issue name. Two recovery points need to be distinguished here.

The recovery point for the media branch is the original CSS example and the test location for `parse-serialize.spec.ts`. If the newly added example itself is unreliable, returning to the original example is enough to reestablish a local comparison. The two import statements at the top of the file can help the person taking over confirm that the test side still uses `../parse-css` and `../serialize-css` as its entry points.

The cross-document branch does not have an equally fixed file-level recovery point. Its recovery targets should be the entry point, version, and actual results for the confirmed caller; when the caller has not yet been found, this page cannot identify a specific file to roll back. In that situation, the safest state is not to pretend that rollback steps already exist, but to keep the status as "caller not confirmed".

This also explains why the two tracks cannot be modified together. Rolling back a media example means rolling back test materials. A rollback for a cross-document case must be tied to the actual caller. Both can appear in the same round of compatibility checks, but neither can substitute for the other.

## 2025: what the card brought back was not a conclusion

AUR-204 retained the two search patterns `parseCss`, `serializeCss` for pseudo-class nesting within media, and required adding repository tests based on examples from user reports, preserving the failing text or output bytes. This made test-side searching more direct, but did not automatically supply the inputs missing from the old records.

The records for 2025-09-23 included one rollback check. Here, rollback only means that the old samples and old entry points must still be recoverable, not that a releasable fix already exists. By 2025-10-07, this track was blocked again because the input fields had not yet been confirmed. This status indicates that the samples still lack the materials needed to turn them into reviewable tests; an import in the test file cannot be treated as proof that verification is complete.

AUR-220 documents inconsistent results in Cross-document Constructable Stylesheets's user environment. 2025-10-28 recorded a counterexample. The counterexample changed the earlier optimistic assessment: we can no longer assume that two objects share a parser path just because they belong to the same compatibility train. The counterexample did not provide the caller version, creation entry point, or current results, so it did not narrow the cross-document branch down to a file-level conclusion either.

The two cards work well as side-by-side navigation: AUR-204 points to media samples and test materials, AUR-220 points to the caller's cross-document environment. They should not be merged into a single "CSS parser issue".

The adjacent DOC-16 deals with whitespace text nodes during hydration and CSS content escape Fidelity. It can serve as navigation to nearby compatibility samples, but it cannot replace the records here on media nesting or constructable stylesheet entry points.

## Migration path currently in use

The current work no longer requires the two tracks to converge at the outset. First preserve the originals, then follow their respective branches based on the materials:

```text
Original style fragment
  |
  +-- pseudo-class nesting inside media
  |     |
  |     +-- parse-serialize.spec.ts
  |            |
  |            +-- parseCss
  |            +-- serializeCss
  |            +-- Save the input and output text
  |
  +-- Cross-document Constructable Stylesheets
        |
        +-- Find callers still in use
               |
               +-- Verify the actual version
               +-- Verify the entry point
               +-- Keep the current result
```

The two branches in the diagram are not two sets of unrelated rules, but two different starting points. The media branch starts from the comparable CSS; the cross-document branch starts from the caller that actually uses the stylesheet. Only when the latter confirms that its style payload has a comparable relationship to the former should we continue discussing whether the same compatibility adjustment is needed.

Before migrating the media example, check whether the input is still raw text. If what you received is already a serialized result, note that in the record; do not treat it as parser input. After migration, retain the input and output text; if there is no output, record whether the process stopped on the parser side or the serializer side. This way, the next review can at least continue from a known point instead of starting over by guessing from the page's appearance.

Before migrating the cross-document example, first confirm that the caller is still using a constructable stylesheet. Then record its version, entry point, and current result. The current material does not provide a specific caller file, so this page does not fabricate a path for it. If the caller has not yet been located, retain only the current-state description and card navigation.

When restoring the old media path, restore the original CSS example and the test location for `parse-serialize.spec.ts`. When restoring the old cross-document path, restore the state of the confirmed caller; without a caller, there is no executable file-level restoration action. Do not copy the restoration point from the previous item to the latter.

## Current requirements for the media branch

After the previous old plan, split records, review addendum, and card counterexample, the media branch adopts the following requirement:

> `parseCss` and `serializeCss` must retain nested pseudo-class selectors inside the media block and output a compact CSS with no diagnostics and equivalent semantics.

This statement applies only to this type of CSS input within media blocks. When verifying, check the nested pseudo-class relationships, whether any diagnostics are emitted, whether the output preserves the same semantics, and whether the output is compact CSS. It does not designate Cross-document Constructable Stylesheets as downstream of these two functions, nor does it supply a caller for AUR-220.

If a media example fails to meet this requirement, first save the original input and actual output, then determine whether the discrepancy lies in the observed parsing behavior or the serialized text. If there are not enough output artifacts, stop at what can be proven, and do not use cross-document results as counterevidence or as passing results.

## Related issues retained here rather than split out

The input fields for AUR-204 are still unconfirmed. This gap prevents the user-reported examples from being reliably included in test comparisons, but it does not change the direct dependencies visible in the file header. Do not describe "there is an import" as "reproducible input is already available".

The counterexample for AUR-220 still lacks the actual caller, version, and entry point. It shows that the old assumption of a unified path is unreliable, but it does not establish whether the cross-document result occurs in the parser, the serializer, or the code that uses constructable stylesheets. Once the caller is found, first document the case under the cross-document branch, then determine whether it is worth comparing with the media example.

# Migration Steps for CSS Module Comment Cleanup

The initial recorded location was very specific: both the issue name and the call name led to `internal/aurora-core`'s `v_prev`, at the path `src/compiler/style/css-to-esm.ts`. This location is still retained here, not because it has been proven that this file cleans up the comments, but because the old investigation started here, and later records also need to be able to return to the same starting point.

The old notes once described a "path match" almost as if it established where the implementation belonged. That was the working judgment at the time: the filename, the issue name related to CSS and the call name appeared together, so opening this file first was the easiest option. This judgment has not been erased, but it is no longer sufficient as the result of a compatibility check. A file location can provide an entry point for reading, but cannot replace the result of a call.

## Nearby Functionality at the Old Entry Point

The following imports are directly visible at the top of `css-to-esm.ts`:

```ts
import {
  catchError,
  createJsVarName,
  DEFAULT_STYLE_MODE,
  hasError,
  isString,
  normalizePath,
  resolve,
} from '@utils';
```

The early investigation conflated these nearby pieces of functionality with "where comment cleanup happens". Looking back now, all that can be said is that they are visible within the same file. The names `catchError` and `hasError` alone cannot prove that a particular failed call passed through here; nor can the import of `scopeCss` alone prove that it caused a change in comments. The old wording is retained so that whoever takes over knows why the investigation started from this path at the time, rather than sanitizing it into a precise conclusion reached only later.

## What Is Moving Is Not a Source File

This migration does not involve any confirmed relocation of source code. The available material provides no new implementation path, nor does it identify a file to replace `css-to-esm.ts`. What actually changes is the focus of the verification records: from "there is an old file entry point", to "the same check has two visible call results".

```text
Issue name / Call name

src/compiler/style/css-to-esm.ts  (old entry point)
        |
        v
Select call samples, retain the actual results
        |

Successful call     Failed call
```
