# Trade-offs for custom elements type exports

When this page was recorded in May, there was only a very narrow starting point: the custom elements Root Type Exports issue would lead searches to `src/compiler/output-targets/dist-custom-elements/index.ts`. The directory name looked enough like an answer, especially when scope had to be set quickly for the compatibility train; but it also looked like the kind of answer that could set the wrong scope. The earliest draft therefore did not identify the file as a public type root, noting only that it was a file the earlier investigation could lead to.

That draft was not intended to deny the relationship between the directory and the output target. Its concern was something more specific: a path match, a module's location, and public declarations are not facts at the same level. If the path were first promoted to a root export, any subsequent type differences would be interpreted as changes to public declarations based on that assumption. If a difference ultimately affected only one output, the scope of changes would be much larger than the actual problem.

## The file header visible at the time

The excerpt of the file header was never completed. What remained at the beginning was `import {`, followed by:

```ts
import ts from 'typescript';
import type * as d from '../../../declarations';
import type { BundleOptions } from '../../bundle/bundle-interface';
```

These lines are not an export definition, but pointers to three local connections. `typescript` is a value import; `d` is an import of declaration types; `BundleOptions` comes from the bundle interface. They show that this file sits close to compilation processing, declaration types, and bundling options. In May, there were no complete import entries, no export snippets, and no consumer examples, so none of the names was presented as the formal name of a "type root".

Initially, some favored recording it directly by directory name: since the path was under `output-targets/dist-custom-elements/`, the root export should be assigned here. This wording was short and easy to check off in the train checklist. The alternative was more restrained: keep the path as a starting point for verification, first find the references in that revision, and then check whether the output had actually changed.

The latter choice is what is ultimately recorded here. The decision was not about "whether this file is important", but about "whether the directory and file header alone are enough to define it as a root type export". The answer was that it could not be defined directly on that basis. This adds a reference check, but does not turn a search result into a public contract.

## The earlier judgment retained in the initial draft

The May version took a simple practical approach: do not reassign the file up front; do not treat the directory name as a public interface; wait until the previous round's usable results and the current declarations are brought together before defining the scope. The text at the time did not list function names or speculate about the specific purpose of `d`. This limited judgment is retained now because it explains why the export description was not later corrected directly on the basis of the filename.

This also means the old draft did not provide a complete implementation description. It did not say where consumers read types from, did not list the file structure of the final artifacts, let alone name a job. None of that information was on this page at the time. The early record merely put a premature attribution on hold to prevent it from spreading further through the compatibility train.

## The unit of comparison adopted after review

Later review changed the question from "is this directory the root export" to "where exactly do the results differ". The local description for AUR-211 calls for checking custom elements Root Type Exports against the previous round's usable artifacts, and updating only the jobs or pinned versions that actually changed. This scope is much narrower than a directory-based judgment, and is better suited to the regression checks for R26.9.

"Only update" has two meanings here. First, a path match is not a reason to include all custom elements-related outputs in the changes. Second, an unchanged job name is not a reason to ignore differences in results that a pinned version may introduce. The material provides neither specific job names nor specific pinned versions, so this page does not invent names; it preserves the comparison method, not an apparently complete table of results.

Imports in the file header and artifact differences must not be conflated into a single judgment either. The former help point back to declarations and bundle configuration, while the latter determine which results actually need to be checked in this round. A value import does not imply a public type export, and a type import does not imply that an artifact has already regressed. Separating these signals is the clearest narrowing of scope on this page between May and the review stage.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> FilePath
    FilePath --> ReferenceCheck
    ReferenceCheck --> ArtifactComparison
    ArtifactComparison --> RetainUnconfirmedItems
    RetainUnconfirmedItems --> [*]
```

The sequence in the diagram is not a new implementation workflow, but the order of evaluation used in this record. The path is still useful, but it only gets us as far as a reference check; before the artifacts are compared, the directory name is not written up as a conclusion about the export.

## Wording not adopted

The difference between the two sentences considered can be seen side by side:

- "`src/compiler/output-targets/dist-custom-elements/index.ts` is custom elements Root Type Exports."
- "`src/compiler/output-targets/dist-custom-elements/index.ts` is the starting file for the current follow-up investigation of custom elements Root Type Exports."

The first sentence conflates location and assignment. It reads like a conclusion, but leaves out what still needs to be aligned between declarations, references, and outputs. The second sentence does not try to replace the subsequent checks, nor does it imply that every type difference requires changing this file. R26.9 uses the wording of the second sentence on this page.

The cost of this decision is that reviewers cannot stop at the directory listing. They need to first examine the file's local connections to `typescript`, `../../../declarations`, and `../../bundle/bundle-interface`, then bring the references they find back into the comparison with the results from the previous round's usable artifacts. The benefit is that scope is narrowed by actual differences, rather than expanded by similarly named directories.

The first sentence was not adopted, not because it necessarily contradicts the eventual implementation, but because it is too categorical given the material available. Even if a public type were later confirmed to originate in this area, there was not enough information in May to state that definitively. The decision record preserves the boundary that was actionable at the time: treat the path as a starting point first, not the starting point as a definition.

## A counterexample added in October

For AUR-211, an action serving as a counterexample was recorded on 2025-10-02, followed by a brief note in the record: there was still one unconfirmed point for custom elements Root Type Exports. This brief note did not identify a symbol, file, or result, nor did it provide a second export that could be recorded. It cannot be expanded into "a second root export has been found".

But it changed how this page was wrapped up. The May version only said to wait for a comparison; after review, the record can explicitly retain one still-unconfirmed relationship, with the confirmation step placed where the current declarations, actual references, and the previous round's usable artifacts meet. The directory name cannot fill this gap, nor can additional speculation about imports.

The counterexample from that same day does not conflict with the earlier misreading of the directory. The former shows that there are still gaps in the checks, while the latter shows that file location cannot replace checking. Together, these two points constrain what can be said in this round: do not claim to have fully established where it belongs, do not extend the scope to other output targets, and do not present unspecified consumer relationships as established facts.

The record from 2025-10-03 shows that this check moved from To Do to In Progress. This transition is retained here to show that the unconfirmed item was not treated as complete in that record; it does not itself provide new export symbols or artifact results, so no further conclusions are drawn from it.

## Decision record for R26.9

The R26.9 Compatibility Train handles custom elements Root Type Exports as follows:

1. `src/compiler/output-targets/dist-custom-elements/index.ts` is retained as the local starting point for verification.
2. `import ts from 'typescript';`, `import type * as d from '../../../declarations';`, and `import type { BundleOptions } from '../../bundle/bundle-interface';` are used only as clues to local connections visible in the file header, not recorded as descriptions of public exports.
3. When comparing against the previous round's usable artifacts, only jobs or pinned versions that have actually changed are included in this round's change scope.
4. With one relationship still unconfirmed, do not claim to have fully established where custom elements Root Type Exports belongs.

These four points are not a new output-target design. They only specify how this compatibility train records and scopes changes with the material currently available. The path can still be searched, imports can still help pinpoint locations, and actual differences can still be brought into the checks; none of these can replace the other two on its own.

## A starting point for the next review

If specific references become available later, they should be added between "FilePath" and "ArtifactComparison", rather than using the directory name again to open up a broader conclusion. If all that appears is another similar directory match, continue to follow this page's decision: first confirm its relationship to the declarations and outputs, then determine whether it affects the scope of R26.9.

When you need to return to this page, you can find this check via AUR-211; the card preserves local regression clues, while this page preserves the choice made at the time between the two wordings.

# shadow boolean attribute proposal

The initial draft reduced this issue to "declaration presence is equivalent to attribute presence." That statement remains in the history above, but it was only an assumption made at the time to move the trial forward. It should not be treated as the existing interface contract. No comparable failure text or output bytes were supplied during review, so that assumption cannot be used to explain the examples in the user report.

## Scope for this round

The discussion is about shadow boolean attributes in component declarations, not arbitrary HTML boolean attributes. The two may look the same in text but may not carry the same information before reaching the runtime. If the trial treats them as identical, even passing tests cannot show whether the declaration entry point preserves the distinction between "not provided" and "provided as false."

The initial draft also assumed that the change belonged on the accessor side. That remains a candidate location, but is no longer a decision about where the change belongs: the declaration entry point, test fixtures, and accessor may each be only one link in the reproduction chain. R26.9 needs a narrowly scoped change that can be covered by consumer examples, not a reworking of all attribute rules as part of this issue.

## Possible trial paths

| Path | What it aims to verify | Main cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pass declaration values directly to the existing accessor | Whether the existing attribute-setting logic can preserve differences in boolean inputs | Must first confirm that the accessor has not already collapsed its handling of default values, false, and name presence |
| Preserve declaration inputs separately in the test fixture | First capture the form used in the report alongside the final output | Does not yet establish how the production declaration entry point should be wired in |
| Do not add declaration mapping | Retain only the reproduction and wait for input semantics to be clarified | R26.9 will not cover the compatibility expectations for this example |

The first path is still a lower-cost candidate, but its prerequisite is stricter than the initial draft stated: tests cannot just assert whether an attribute is present at the end. On failure, they must also make it possible to tell whether the input was missing, false, or in name form before reaching the accessor. The second path is suitable while that prerequisite remains unverified. It is not a long-term solution; it only avoids reducing the user report to an assertion that discards the input's original state.

## Review starting point

This review only revisited the immediate connections around `src/runtime/vdom/test/set-accessor.spec.ts`. This test file directly imports `BUILD` and, from `../set-accessor`, imports `parseClassList` and `setAccessor`. So when adding examples next time, we can start near this group of tests and check whether the existing fixtures can construct declaration inputs, and whether the value received by `setAccessor` still preserves the distinction between the three states above.

Here, `BUILD` is not treated as a switch for shadow behavior. At this point it is simply a dependency already present in the test file; if the example changes only under a particular build condition, the condition and output should be recorded separately and must not be inferred from the import location.

## What to retain during the trial

The example from the report needs to be saved as a separate sample, along with the failure text or output bytes from that time. Simply writing "boolean is wrong" is not specific enough: the declaration might not have been passed in, it might have been normalized after being passed in, or the assertion might be observing a different layer.

If the first path is chosen, the minimal change should first meet two requirements: an omitted declaration must not be turned into true; an explicit false must not be overridden because the attribute name is present. The available material does not settle whether the attribute should ultimately be removed, written, or retained only in component state, and the trial notes must not make that decision.

The initial draft's statement that "using the existing accessor is enough" should now be considered outdated. Its remaining value is to explain why a smaller change was initially preferred: the interface review raised concerns that adding a branch would pull declarative examples away from the ordinary attribute path. The connections around the tests found during review are not enough to support that commitment.

## Withdrawal and open questions

Withdraw the attempt to integrate R26.9 if any of the following occurs: the reproduction cannot reliably preserve the original input; the existing accessor has already collapsed missing and false into one state; or the test can only assert the formatted HTML, with no way to locate where in the chain the state is lost. When withdrawing, retain the reproduction and failure output, and do not leave a temporary conversion in the declaration entry point.

Questions still unanswered: what the name shadow covers in the reported example; whether the consumer expects to observe component state or DOM; and whether there is already a nearby Component Exclusion Wildcards issue that would share the test fixtures. The last item is not grounds for handling the issues together; it only needs to be considered when scheduling the review to keep the two from obscuring each other.

# template content Mounting Integration Guide

The migration covers the entry points and fields of compatibility check records, not runtime code. The legacy records already tie issue names, call names and `src/runtime/vdom/util.ts` together; later reviews showed that file paths can only serve as lookup references, not establish who handles mounting for a caller. The current approach carries over the old clues, but lets the new call context determine whether tracing can continue.

## Preserve the legacy route first

The legacy route has practical value. If someone remembers only "template content Mounting", or only part of a call name, they can use the original terms to retrieve historical entries. The template forms, mounting results and description order already present in legacy entries must also be retained, because they capture the context before migration, and must not be rewritten to reflect later accounts.

When opening the file pointed to by the legacy route, record only the directly visible adjacencies:

```ts
import type * as d from '@stencil/core/declarations';
import { NODE_TYPE } from '../runtime-constants';
import { newVNode } from './h';
```

The type declarations, `NODE_TYPE` and `newVNode` can help readers locate this small section of context. They cannot by themselves establish which object determines how template content is mounted, nor can they automatically turn an issue name and call name into a complete call chain. If a legacy record describes this file as the handling location, that sentence should remain in the historical material, but the source-code status in the new entry should be changed to "Legacy tracing entry point".

Use the following format to organize legacy entry points:

| Legacy field | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| Issue name | Keep unchanged for future searches |
| Call name | Keep unchanged, without substituting it for the current call |
| Template form | Copy it separately if recorded, otherwise leave it missing |
| Mounting result | Retain the description from that time, without inferring it from the path |
| Source-code location | Record `src/runtime/vdom/util.ts` as the legacy entry point |

When a legacy entry has no template form, do not infer the template structure from a result such as "the user saw empty content"; when a legacy entry has no result, do not fill the result field with `newVNode` or a node type either. The first step in migration is to preserve missing fields, not make legacy entries look complete.

## Connect the current call

The current route starts with the actual call from AUR-214. The card needs to identify the actual call in the most recent report of template content Mounting and add how the call was made and the result seen by the user. The "current call" here must come from the call context in that report, and cannot be replaced with the call name from a legacy entry.

During AUR-214, `toolchain_pinned` came first, followed by `work_started`. These two items indicate only the stage of work at the time of the review: the toolchain had been locked down, and processing had begun. They are not evidence of successful mounting, matching results or a connection to the source code, so they belong only in the work context of the migration record, not in the result field.

Create new entries in this order:

1. **Preserve the call wording.** Keep the description of how the call was made in the current report unchanged. If only a name can be confirmed, enter only that name in the field, without adding parameters, template structure or a caller based on experience.
2. **Preserve the user result.** Record the mounting result the user actually saw, separately from how the call was made. If the result does not appear in the report, write "Result pending"; do not treat adjacent objects in the source code as user results.
3. **Continue tracing.** Follow source-code references from the current call, and check whether they connect to `src/runtime/vdom/util.ts`. If you can only open the file without an actual reference relationship, set the status to "Path pending confirmation".
4. **Place the legacy record alongside it.** Keep the legacy call, current call and their respective results separate. Merge them into a single compatibility check only when the content on both sides can be matched to the same behavior.

```text
Legacy issue name / Legacy call name ──┬── Legacy template form (if any)
                      ├── Legacy mounting result (if any)
                      └── util.ts Legacy tracing entry point

Current actual call ──────────┬── How the call is made
                       ├── Result seen by the user
                       └── Whether actual references connect to util.ts

When the two sides correspond: proceed to comparison
When either side has missing fields: preserve the missing fields, do not merge
```

"Path pending confirmation" and "Inconsistent descriptions" must be distinguished. The former means the current call has not yet been connected to source-code references; the latter means the call or result has been obtained, but the two sources describe it differently. Neither case may be marked "Compared".

## Migrate in batches

Do not update all legacy entries at once. Process them in three batches according to how complete the material is.

**First batch: calls are available on both sides.** First select entries where the legacy entry has a call name and the current record also has an actual call. Ask only two questions when comparing them: whether they describe the same call context, and whether the user results can be matched item by item. If they correspond, add the source-code tracing location to the same record; if not, retain both descriptions and do not force a merge.

**Second batch: only legacy results are available.** These entries can retain the legacy issue name, legacy call name and legacy mounting result, but the current call field should say "Pending". Even if they all point to `src/runtime/vdom/util.ts`, do not reuse current calls from the first batch. The same file does not mean the same template form, much less the same caller.

**Third batch: only a current report is available.** When the current report provides a call or result but no reliable legacy counterpart can be found, create a separate current entry. Do not place it under the most similar legacy issue name. If legacy material is found later, it can be added alongside the legacy fields; until then, the current entry retains its own call and result.

Perform only one local check for each batch: whether the current call and user result come from the same source; whether the legacy result actually exists in the legacy entry; whether the source-code location was obtained by continuing to trace from the call, or merely found through legacy keywords. Do not conflate these three things. In particular, do not mark an entry without a result as having passed compatibility simply because AUR-214 has already entered `work_started`.

## How to restore the legacy path

Restoration here does not mean switching runtime code, nor does it mean undoing the call wording already preserved. It means: when there is insufficient correspondence along the new route, return the entry to the legacy search entry point and wait for the missing material to be supplied.

Restore it in the following situations:

- The current call has only a name, with no result seen by the user;
- The legacy record has only a mounting result, with no comparable call information;

# Postmortem: Unmerged Caller Integration Test Records

The initial snapshot was limited: the same entry point for adj-testing showed two revisions, both labeled `current revision`. The caller had been checking against the old record, but the other record at the entry point had different build conditions. At the time, the available material did not establish which record should be used or show that the two records came from the same update.

Further retries were stopped, and the versions visible at the entry point were saved. This did not withdraw either revision, nor did it mean recovery was complete; it only kept the changing entry-point display from obscuring the initial differences. The earlier draft put the recovery after configuration normalization near the beginning, making it read as though the cause had already been found. That was the working assessment at the time. It is retained, but is no longer treated as a causal explanation.

## Impact

The entry point used for decisions during caller integration testing was directly affected. When the build conditions did not match the old record, the caller could not decide which record to continue with based on `current revision` alone. The caller path later recovered, but that does not establish that the two revisions had been merged or that the full scope of use of the old record had been identified.

The available material supports only the entry-point state for adj-testing, the deviation in build conditions, and a single recovery. There is no material showing the same anomaly in adjacent projects, so changes elsewhere are not included in the causal explanation. Why dependency imports changed remains unknown; the change could be in the same part of the chain as the build conditions, or it could simply be another change that occurred in parallel.

## A Contradiction That Surfaced Later

A more specific timing conflict later surfaced in the comparison records: `original input` had been rolled back, but the action due to run still pointed to the new artifact. This shows, at a minimum, that references to different points in time remained in the same comparison. This item alone still cannot establish when the dual-version state began or explain which record was actually used.

The earlier explanation that simply attributed the anomaly to build conditions needs to be narrowed. Build conditions were the first visible deviation and are useful for comparison; they are not a confirmed root cause. In particular, with an action still pointing to the new artifact after the original input was rolled back, a single difference in conditions can no longer account for how all these records relate.

## Leads Added Later

| Record | Open issue at the time | Known status |
|---|---|---|
| AURB-004 | Choose one adjacent `current revision` with a working path and compare only the first path difference | Scope confirmed; later handed off to those responsible for interface compatibility for confirmation |
| AURB-005 | Exit actions missing from both versions of the records | Withdrawal commands or stop conditions need to be added; progress was blocked at one point because the test machine was occupied by other regression tests |
| AURB-006 | Teams still using adj-testing at the end remain to be confirmed | A baseline record was saved; the scope of use remains unconfirmed |
| AURB-007 | Tracing the source of `testing-client-integration` | Tracing back through revisions to the earliest reconstructable source has begun, and the work has entered security triage |

AURB-004 was deliberately narrow in scope: compare only the first path difference in one adjacent record. This limit does not mean later differences do not exist; it avoids bundling the build conditions, import changes, and display state into a single explanation. The lead was later handed to the person responsible for interface compatibility for confirmation, indicating that the comparison approach was clear, not that a conclusion on merging had been reached.

AURB-005 exposed a gap distinct from recovery. Further retries were stopped at the time to preserve the differences; exiting requires a withdrawal command or an explicit stop condition. The original incident record included no actual withdrawal details. When the test machine was tied up with other regression tests, this line of work could not proceed, so "retries were stopped at the time" cannot be described as having a complete exit procedure in place.

The baseline record left by AURB-006 is not a list of users. It only provided a starting point for finding teams still using adj-testing. The card includes a reminder: `original input` and `current result` are not from the same run and cannot be compared directly. This reminder also limits judgments about the scope of use; the old input and the results after the later recovery cannot be treated as the same batch of caller samples.

The direction of work for AURB-007 differs from the adjacent-path comparison. It calls for tracing back through the revisions of `testing-client-integration` to the earliest reconstructable source, rather than guessing the source from the entry-point display text. Entering security triage and starting work only mean this line of inquiry was picked up; they do not mean a security issue has been found or that the provenance chain is complete.

## Earlier Assessments Retained for Now

> The issue cleared after configuration normalization, so the dual-version entry point can be treated as a stale display artifact.

This statement helped bring retries to a stop at the time, but "stale display artifact" is not supported by the material. What is known is that the caller path recovered after configuration normalization; what remains unknown is how two revisions appeared simultaneously at the same entry point, why dependency imports changed, and whether any teams are still using the old record.

Another early statement was "The different build conditions are the cause." It, too, should be retained as an earlier assessment, not as the present conclusion. Different build conditions show that the old record and the entry-point record cannot be aligned directly; they do not explain how the records were written alongside each other.

## Items Carried Forward

- The incident began with two `current revision` entries present at the same entry point.
- Recovery of the caller path after configuration normalization is an observed result.
- `original input` had already been rolled back, yet the action due to run still pointed to the new artifact: a time/state conflict recorded later.
- Dependency imports, exit actions, the last users, and the provenance chain all remain open questions.

The entry point for the material remains `docs/adj-testing/incidents/testing-client-integration-two-record-versions-not-merged.md`. DOC-33 retains the migration index for the old entry point; that migration index is not treated here as an explanation for this anomaly.

# Postmortem on Unmerged Caller Integration Testing Records

This record preserves the state of a caller integration testing session whose records were not cleanly merged. Two revisions once appeared at the entry point at the same time, and both records were called `current revision`. Later, the caller's path was restored, and source tracing and a search for the final consumer were started separately; these changes did not automatically merge the two records into one.

The earliest draft said only, "The build conditions differ from those in the old record." This sentence still explains why the anomaly attracted attention, but it does not adequately explain the subsequent handling. The build conditions represented one deviation, not the full evidence for two revisions existing side by side, and they cannot substitute for an explanation of the changes to dependency imports. The old draft remains in the history, but is no longer the sole basis for determining the cause.

## The Earliest Fragment Retained

> adj-testing once placed the `current revision` for two revisions at the same entry point. Recovery is possible through configuration normalization, but why dependency imports changed is still unknown.

This passage squeezed three different things together: the entry point's state, a recovery action, and an unexplained change. The subsequent reorganization did not delete it, but instead separated the subjects.

The entry point's state was that the same integration testing entry point contained records for two different revisions, and both appeared as `current revision`. Here, "the same entry point" means the entry point the caller saw when accessing the integration testing records. It does not mean that the two revisions have been proven to have been written by the same operation, nor does it mean that either record has been confirmed obsolete.

The recovery action was the restoration of the caller's path after configuration normalization. Recovery did occur, so it can be recorded as a point in the incident; the materials do not explain which internal difference the normalization addressed, nor do they explain whether it would work repeatedly for all adopters. Describing it as "path restored" is closer to the facts recorded at the time than describing it as "problem solved".

The unknown is why dependency imports changed. There was no answer during the initial session, and the subsequent materials did not supply one either. The dependency imports may be in the same segment of the chain as the build conditions, or they may simply be another change that occurred at the same time; this postmortem cannot establish a causal link between the two.

## Where the Assessment Broke Down

The caller could originally follow the old record to cross-check during integration testing. After two instances of `current revision` remained at the entry point simultaneously, the build conditions in the old record differed from those in the other record at the entry point. Continuing to refresh the entry point would only produce a new display state and could not answer whether the old record still applied, so further retries were stopped at that point.

Stopping retries did not mean recovery. It first preserved the records from when the divergence occurred, preventing the results organized later from overwriting the initial entry point state. Nor was it a rollback command: the old materials did not retain the contents of any rollback that had actually been executed, and it was not until the exit actions for the two versions of the records were raised separately later that it became clear this gap remained.

Based on the available materials, the impact first affected the caller's assessment. The caller could not decide which record to continue cross-checking against simply by looking at `current revision`. After the path was restored, this obstacle did not necessarily continue to appear in every integration testing session; however, recovery did not mean that the two versions of the records at the entry point had been merged, much less that the scope of adoption had been accounted for.

No materials state that other projects were affected by the same anomaly at the same time. This page records only the dual-version state at the adj-testing entry point, the deviation in build conditions, the recovery after configuration normalization, and the follow-up investigations that were later pursued separately. No inferences are made here about the behavior of neighboring projects.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Caller integration testing entry point] --> B[Two revision entries side by side]
    B --> C[Both marked as the current revision]
    C --> D[Retain the records seen at the entry point]
    D --> E[Path restored after configuration normalization]
    B --> F[Continue tracing provenance by revision]
```

The diagram does not connect "path restored" to "records merged". The two happened in sequence during the incident, but they are not the same conclusion. The dual-version state concerns the entry-point object; recovery is the outcome for a single caller path.

## Sequence of early actions

| Stage | What was observed at the time | What was left on record |
|---|---|---|
| Initial discovery | The build conditions for the old record differed from those for the other record at the entry point | Preserved the two revision entries side by side |
| Before further checks | It was unclear which `current revision` the caller should use | Stopped repeated retries and saved the versions seen at the entry point |
| At recovery | The caller path recovered after configuration normalization | Recorded the recovery time separately from confirmation of the cause |
| Follow-up comparison | The `original input` had been rolled back, but the expiration action still pointed to the new artifact | The earlier attribution solely to build conditions was narrowed |
| Still under investigation | Dependency imports, exit actions, scope of adoption, and the provenance chain | Each remained a separate follow-up item, rather than being grouped together as resolved |

This table is not a complete operational log. It only lists the changes actually documented in the materials. The initial draft left one timestamp blank; it was not later filled in with an exact time, because the materials did not provide the full intervals between the initial discovery, stopping retries, and configuration normalization.

Separating the time of recovery from the time of root-cause confirmation was the most important correction made during the later write-up. The earlier draft put "configuration normalization enables recovery" immediately before "it is unclear why the dependency imports changed", making it easy to read the former as already explaining the latter. The actual situation was more limited: the former was the result of an action, while the latter remained an unanswered question.

## Build conditions: still useful, but not the cause

The first visible discrepancy was that the build conditions differed from those in the old record. This observation remains valid: it shows that when the caller was making decisions based on the old record, the entry point was already no longer providing the same conditions. It is also why the two records could no longer be treated as directly interchangeable versions during the incident.

But "different build conditions" does not establish why the records appeared side by side. It does not explain how the two revision entries entered the same entry point, does not explain which one had been updated, and does not explain why the expiration action still pointed to the new artifact. The earlier version presented it too much as the cause, and this broader interpretation later had to be retracted.

The old wording is retained below:

> The build conditions are already different, so just proceed with the new entry point for now.

This statement later ceased to apply. The new entry point itself was part of the incident; when the entry point retained two records marked `current revision`, "the entry point is newer" could not substitute for confirming the relationship between the versions. This wording once made it easier to move forward during the incident, but it would lose the distinction between the old record and the entry-point record.

This does not mean the build conditions are irrelevant. They remain one of the earliest items to show differences when comparing adjacent records, and one of the best places to look first. The later decision to compare only the first path difference was also specifically intended to avoid attributing changes beyond the build conditions to this same factor.

## Recovery after configuration normalization

After configuration normalization, the caller path recovered. The postmortem retains this statement as a positive result, but does not extend it into the current operating practice.

The recovery shows that, in that incident, the normalized configuration was compatible with the caller path. It does not show that the entry states of the two revisions were corrected, nor that, if the same presentation is encountered in the future, the same action should be repeated directly. The materials contain neither the complete configuration contents before and after normalization, nor repeated samples, nor a list of adopters.

The early draft made "path recovery" a sentence close to a conclusion because the caller could already continue at the time. Looking back now, this brought only one path at the time to an end; it did not resolve the three items in the postmortem: why the records for the two versions were side by side, why dependency imports changed, and which teams might still adopt one of the versions.

Therefore, this page still retains the word "recovery," but does not use "fixed" to describe the entire anomaly. Recovery refers to an observed result; the fact that the two-version records were not merged is a separate issue that remains unresolved.

## Rollback and the pointer to the new artifact were not synchronized

In the public record for AURB-004, it was written: `original input` had been rolled back, while the expiration action still pointed to the new artifact. This phenomenon is more specific than the initial deviation from the build conditions, because it leaves two different temporal states side by side in the same comparison.

Here, "expiration action" cannot be interpreted as a release mechanism that was not provided, nor can "new artifact" be used to infer that all adopters have migrated. What can be confirmed is that the rolled-back original input and the action pointing to the new artifact were not synchronized. This undermines the basis for the old judgment that "the entry was merely a display remnant," and also means that the two versions being side by side can no longer be explained by a single build difference alone.

The original task for AURB-004 was to select an adjacent `current revision` with a path that could be followed, comparing only the first path difference. Once the scope was confirmed, the issue was handed to the person responsible for interface compatibility for confirmation. This handoff indicates that the comparison direction had been constrained; it does not mean that a decision on interface compatibility had already been made.

The role of this clue is to control the comparison scope. When two revisions appear simultaneously, comparing all paths, all build conditions, and all import changes at once would conflate their sequence. Focusing only on the first difference cannot directly identify the root cause, but it can prevent subsequent differences that have not been confirmed from being written up as causes.

An old record once contained another simplification:

> `original input` was rolled back, and the new record naturally took over.

It was later found that the expiration action still pointed to the new artifact, so this statement could no longer stand. The rollback and the pointer to the new artifact were not synchronized; this cannot be treated as "natural takeover," nor can it be used to determine which `current revision` has become invalid.

## The exit action remained incomplete

What AURB-005 proposed was not "run another integration test," but that the records for the two versions lacked an exit action. If there is no rollback command or stop condition after recovery, then the next time the same entry state is encountered, the team on site can only repeat the previous provisional judgment.

In the early response, "stop continuing retries" was a real option, but it was not equivalent to a complete exit action. It did not specify when attempts should resume, nor did it leave a command specifying which record to retract. The later card requires adding a retraction command or a stop condition, which makes clear that this part was not fully documented in the earlier incident context.

This card was once blocked because the test machine was occupied by another regression run. This status only means that validation could not continue on that machine at the time; it does not mean that the dual-version issue was caused by the test machine, nor that the exit action was later completed. If the old postmortem records the test-machine status as the cause of the anomaly, it would conflate the blocking context with the relationship between records.

An earlier version placed "stop continuing retries" beside the recovery narrative, making it easy for readers to interpret a temporary stop as a completed rollback. They are now treated separately: stopping retries protected the current state; the exit action still lacks executable content. AURB-005 remain a navigation point for this gap; they do not indicate that this gap already has an outcome.

## The last consumer is still under investigation

AURB-006 is used to find the teams that still use adj-testing, and requires the search scope to be recorded even if no consumer is found. This requirement itself shows that the scope of adoption was not known when the incident occurred.

That card later left a baseline record, but a baseline record is not a list of consumers. It only provided a starting point for subsequent searching. The current materials do not list any confirmed teams, nor do they support the conclusion "no one is using it", so this page does not broaden the post-recovery path to imply that all callers have migrated.

The same record also notes: `original input` and `current result` are not from the same round and cannot be directly compared. This reminder likewise limits judgments about the scope of adoption. If the old input and the result after later recovery are treated as samples from the same round, changes over time would be misrepresented as changes in consumers.

"The last consumer" is an incident carryover item, not an assignment to any particular team. It is related to the dual-version state at the entry point: if the old record is still in use, whether the entry point is merged will continue to affect the integration-testing assessment; if there is no adopter, the scope already searched still needs to be retained, and the old record cannot be deleted directly based on path restoration alone.

An early simplified statement was, "if the last consumer cannot be found, the old record can be cleared." This is not a requirement of AURB-006. The card requires the search scope to be recorded even when no one is using it; without this scope, it is impossible to distinguish between genuinely having no users and simply not having found one yet.

## Source tracing is still in progress

The goal of AURB-007 is to follow the revision of `testing-client-integration` back to the earliest source that can be reconstructed, rather than guessing from the displayed text. This approach differs from the adjacent-path comparison of AURB-004: the former traces the earliest source in time, while the latter compares the first difference between the two records at hand.

The card entered security triage, and work on it began afterward. The status here only indicates that it entered the corresponding workflow; this page contains no record of a security issue being discovered, nor does it use the triage status to attribute the incident. The results of the provenance investigation are also absent from the available material.

Tracing provenance matters because the two instances of `current revision` displayed at the entry point cannot substitute for revision history itself. Looking only at the entry-point text makes it easy to mistake the current display for the provenance chain; only by tracing back through revision history can we determine where the two records first diverged. The available material does not provide the endpoint of that trace, so provenance remains an open item.

The old draft's tendency to "judge the new record as more credible based on the displayed text" should no longer be used. The displayed text is the surface presentation of the dual-version state, not a standalone basis for determining adoption relationships.

## These cards do not form a single chain to completion

The subsequent material does not form a single, linear remediation workflow. It splits into at least two distinct lines of assessment:

- AURB-004 address the first path difference between adjacent `current revision` entries and hand off interface compatibility confirmation to the corresponding workstream.
- AURB-007 address provenance tracing for `testing-client-integration`, following revision history back to the earliest reconstructible source.

AURB-005 and AURB-006 respectively leave gaps in the exit action and the scope of adoption. Describing all four cards as the same completion step would erase the differences in what they address: a path difference is not provenance, provenance is not withdrawal, and withdrawal is not an inventory of consumers.

Neither line of assessment provides a result stating that "the two revisions have been merged". They provide partial material needed for further assessment. The old postmortem title remains precisely because the subsequent records have not overturned the description that "the two versions of the records have not been merged".

## Inaccurate statements retained

The following statements come from wording used at the time at different stages. They are retained to show how the assessment changed; they should not be treated as current conclusions.

> Recovery occurred after configuration normalization, so the entry-point issue is over.

The inaccuracy lies in equating the recovery of one caller path with the end of the entry-point state. Recovery did occur; it did not prove that the two versions of the records at the entry point had been merged.

> The difference in build conditions is the cause.

The inaccuracy lies in elevating the first observed deviation to the cause. Build conditions remain an important point of comparison, but no material shows that they are sufficient to explain why two `current revision` entries appear side by side.

> Stopping further retries is withdrawal.

The inaccuracy lies in the fact that stopping retries only preserved the state at the time. AURB-005 later explicitly called for a withdrawal command or stop condition, showing that the earlier action cannot substitute for the exit details.

> If no adopters can be found, the old record has no impact.

The inaccuracy is that the search was not yet complete. Finding no consumers and completing the consumer inventory are two different things; AURB-006 require documenting the search scope precisely to avoid this kind of leap.

The common problem with these earlier statements is that they turn partial observations into final judgments. The recovery process provided no basis for broadening the conclusions in this way.

## Narrow conclusions that remain valid

First, the entry point for adj-testing once displayed two revisions simultaneously, and both records were labeled `current revision`. This is itself the subject of the postmortem, not a classification added later for ease of narration.

Second, the mismatch between the build conditions and the old records was the first deviation observed at the scene. It supports comparison, not causal attribution on its own.

Third, the caller path was restored after the configuration was normalized. This supports "recovery occurred", not "the records have been merged" or "the cause has been confirmed".

Fourth, the fact that `original input` had been rolled back while the expiration action still pointed to the new artifact shows that at least some time-related state was out of sync. This needs to be retained alongside the dual-version entry point, but cannot be expanded into an implementation explanation that was never provided.

Fifth, there are still no definitive answers regarding the dependency import changes, the exit action, the last consumer, or the earliest source of `testing-client-integration`.

## Items still on the table

| Item | Available material | What cannot substitute for it |
|---|---|---|
| Relationship between the two versions | Two `current revision` records side by side at the same entry point | Recovery after configuration normalization |
| First path difference | Comparison of adjacent records in AURB-004 | Attributing causes to all differences at once |
| Exit action | AURB-005 require adding a rollback command or a stop condition | Stopping retries at the time |
| Last consumer | Baseline records and search requirements in AURB-006 | The assumption that no consumers were found |
| Earliest source | The direction in AURB-007 for tracing back by revision | Display text at the entry point |
| Dependency import changes | An unresolved item left over from the early incident observations | Deviation in build conditions |

The table's "What cannot substitute for it" does not introduce a new process, but reflects confusion that has already occurred during this anomaly: recovery was used in place of determining whether records had been merged, stopping retries was used in place of an exit action, and display text also nearly took the place of tracing the source. Separating these items is intended to prevent the next record from once again describing actions at different levels as a single outcome.

## Relationship to the old entry point index

DOC-33 retains the migration index for the current and legacy entry points. It is cited here only to make the migration records easier to find; DOC-33 does not serve as an explanation of the cause of this dual-version anomaly.

The incident materials for this page are still in `docs/adj-testing/incidents/testing-client-integration-two-record-versions-not-merged.md`. This path stores the records exported by incident-export and the attachment locations. Earlier drafts repeatedly described this path as the starting point for follow-up work; the path is no longer treated as a conclusion, and only preserves the location of the materials at the time of the anomaly.

AURB-004, AURB-005, AURB-006, AURB-007 likewise only provide additional clues about their respective subjects. They do not imply that they were produced at the same time, nor have they been consolidated into a single completed state. After the caller path was restored, different issues remained in each of the four threads.

## Remaining gaps

The missing timestamps in the initial draft have not been filled in. No materials indicate how much time elapsed between the initial discovery and the stopping of retries, nor do any materials specify the full set of conditions under which configuration normalization was completed. Filling in these details to make the timeline neater would write later speculation back into the initial incident record.

Dependency imports likewise remain a gap. They have not been explained merely because work has begun on follow-up cards. Build conditions, path differences, the provenance chain, and dependency imports may be related, but this page does not have enough records to establish their sequence or causality.

The scope of adoption has not been finalized either. AURB-006 left a baseline and a lookup task, but did not provide a final list of consumers. The old records continue to be referenced precisely because this scope has not been confirmed; they should not be recast as a statement that the migration has been completed.

The initial incident record used "configuration normalization can restore it" as its final line. That line was useful to the caller at the time, but it is not suitable as the final conclusion for this anomaly. The conclusion that can be retained now is narrower: the caller path was restored; this did not prove that the `current revision` records for the two revisions had been fully merged. Deviations in build conditions, unsynchronized rollback and pointers to new artifacts, changes in dependency imports, exit actions, the last consumers, and source tracing should still be retained under their respective subjects.

# Release Automation Window Exit Checklist

This checklist was originally prepared for a relatively short runtime-release-automation window. The old page treated "the last result is still available" and "the temporary bypass has been removed" as a pair, which was convenient in practice: when the window closed, the record was closed out too. Later, handoffs and entry-point changes were added to the same queue, but this approach stayed on the page and was not reworked into release rules.

## Retained Legacy Sequence

The old records required first finding `docs/adj-runtime/release/runtime-release-automation-window-exit-checklist.md`, then reading down from "configuration normalization." Once "dependency import" appeared, maintainers would usually start tearing down the setup; if "minimal reproduction" had not appeared, they would stop.

Those three terms were used so that people on duty could point to the same part of the record during handoff, not to determine whether the entire release was complete. The original window record also treated "configuration normalization" as a signal to continue closing the window. That judgment is retained here: the old window was indeed run on that basis, and it will still turn up when reviewing the state of that window later.

The old window-closing steps were:

1. Copy the last visible result.
2. Remove the permissions and bypasses temporarily added for this window.
3. Check whether the queue is still accepting new work; if it is, undo the exit actions.
4. If no minimal reproduction has appeared, do not clean up the original input.

This sequence makes it easy to mistake "the temporary measures can be removed" for "the release has been confirmed." This page does not replace release sign-off; that has always been handled separately by the relevant owner.

## Checks Added After Handoff

AURC-006 record the confirmation times for the person handing over, the person taking over, and runtime · Release Automation. Once the handoff has been confirmed, someone may continue monitoring the window, but that must not erase the original last result. The person taking over needs to see the state before exit, not a summary tidied up afterward.

AURC-007 keep the timeline for runtime-release-automation separate, with only a link in the daily report. The window-closing record therefore no longer attempts to retell that timeline; at handoff, this page only records which side is still watching the window. If the daily report and this page describe things differently, go back to the separate timeline first; do not add exit details to the daily report.

AURC-008 added a complication to the old procedure: after the current entry point changes, the before-and-after statistics cannot be directly subtracted. In the past, the two numbers recorded before and after window closure were sometimes placed side by side as proof that the window had stabilized. That wording has not been deleted, because the old records were already archived that way; when closing a window now, at a minimum, note alongside the numbers whether the entry point changed. Do not combine the figures from the two periods into a single trend.

## Checklist for This Window

When opening the window:

- [ ] Record the entry point used for this window and the first visible result.
- [ ] Keep one sample of a successful path and one of a rejected path; do not overwrite them with later reruns.
- [ ] If using a read-only account, first confirm whether it is already available. If the account is still awaiting approval, do not proceed to the post-reproduction window-closing steps.
- [ ] Record temporary permissions, bypasses, and queue intake separately; do not lump them together as "environment handled."

When closing the window:

- [ ] Confirm that the last result is still visible before starting to remove temporary permissions.
- [ ] After removing the bypass, check whether the queue is still accepting work for the window. If it is, undo the exit actions already taken and keep the window open.
- [ ] If no minimal reproduction has appeared, retain the original input and the results seen so far; do not clean up the setup just because "dependency import" has appeared.
- [ ] If the entry point changes, mark the records before and after the change separately. Do not subtract them directly or backfill results from the later period into the earlier one.

A read-only account once stalled this checklist partway through. The blocker in AURC-008 was that the account needed for reproduction was still awaiting approval; at that point, even if other projects had already started closing their windows, adj-runtime could only preserve the state and wait. The old version treated the account as a borrowed resource, assuming it would be returned before window closure; in the actual handoff, it became a prerequisite for completing the reproduction. This page was not turned into an account approval workflow on that basis; only a stop point was added here.

## What to Record After Exit

After the exit actions are complete, record just three things: the last visible result, which temporary measures were removed, and whether the entry point changed during the window. Do not include whether the release succeeded, whether scheduling will continue, or the status of other projects in this checklist.

If, after removing permissions, you find that the queue still has new work, revert to the state before permissions were removed and record the result at that point again. If the result is no longer visible, do not fill the gap with a tidied-up green status; keep a record saying "the last result could not be retrieved" and wait for the person taking over to decide whether to reopen the window.

DOC-37 can be used as related reference material when reviewing the current entry point, but the unfinished parts must not be used as grounds for exit under this checklist. AURC-006, AURC-007, and AURC-008 retain the handoff, separate timeline, and entry-point change records, respectively; this page only uses them when the window ends.

The old checklist still treats the window as a limited-scope closeout. This framing may lead people to underestimate the gaps introduced by entry-point switches and account approval, but deleting it would strip past window-closing records of their context. Subsequent windows will therefore continue to use the stop points above, and the old paragraphs will remain.

# Release Automation Roadmap Design

At the time, two different ways of structuring the information were being compared: continuing to pack release information into "metadata folding," or splitting "source mapping" into a separate section. This records the trade-offs of the options that were not adopted; it does not mean either one has become the current entry point for runtime · Release Automation.

## Metadata Folding

This approach would require fewer changes; the build queue would still be organized around `.github/workflows/release`, and artifact versions and the rollback window would continue to be read from the same place. Its proponents believed that, once release records were consolidated, a single metadata view would let you follow the version to the corresponding artifact; for cases that only require confirming whether a particular release entered the queue, this format is relatively straightforward.

The objection was that, once the metadata contained both the source description and the generated result, the two outputs would be conflated. One output would need to answer "what source produced this artifact"; the other would need to answer "whether this version can still be rolled back." The failure paths for these two sections would not be the same; after they were folded together, it would be difficult to tell whether the source was missing or the rollback window had already closed. The older records do not provide enough evidence to show that this issue had already been resolved in the build queue.

## Separate Source Mapping

Another approach would move `source mapping` out of the release metadata and have it describe only the relationship between the source and the build result; version status and rollback determinations would remain in the original release records. If this approach failed, the declaration output could be checked first, followed by a separate check of whether the artifact version exists; the troubleshooting path would be longer, but the object boundaries would be somewhat clearer. The trade-off is that two entry points would have to be maintained, and the compatibility train's current callers would also have to be listed first; otherwise, after the split, only the record format might change, with callers still reading through the old entry point.

The leaning at the time was toward the latter, but it was only a preference at the proposal stage. There was no start date or owner, so the trial cannot be written up as already in effect. A reverse-input case still needs to be added: when the source declaration exists but the artifact version is missing, which section should the issue be assigned to; if rollback fails, is the old entry point sufficient for recovery, or must source mapping also be restored? This validation window was not closed in this record.

## Rollback Points for Deferred Adoption

If, after the trial, it turns out that callers in the compatibility train still depend on the folded fields, restore the old entry point before deleting the existing release records. If the only issue is that source mapping cannot be generated, retain the version record and mark the mapping gap; the two cases must not be represented by the same "release failed" result. After that, only the reverse-input case and caller list need to be added before deciding whether to advance this approach from proposal to an actual change.

The materials entry point remains `docs/adj-runtime/proposals/rejected-runtime-release-automation-approach.md`. Results from adjacent pages are not backfilled into this record.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Dependency Boundary Blockers

Start from the current entry point. First record the symptoms actually visible on the page; do not start by treating this as "a problem with the dependency source." This flow follows only one branch of dev-server-supply-boundary; stop wherever new evidence is needed.

## Starting Point

If the entry page lets you locate a minimal reproduction, retain that reproduction and the first failing sample. Earlier records include cases of retrying first and then going back to find samples, by which point environmental differences had been overwritten. Do not use that approach again.

- If the page displays a style payload, preserve the page state first. Do not clean up the environment or switch to another payload to continue testing.
- If there is no style payload, go back to the minimal reproduction. If there is no reproducible behavior at the entry point, do not proceed to the source assessment below.

## Branches

**A minimal reproduction exists and the style payload is visible**

Continue looking for the build conditions. If the build conditions are already visible, use them to confirm which dev-server-supply-boundary this display corresponds to; if old and new relationships are mixed together, examine the two relationships separately. An old link must not override the chain currently visible.

If the build conditions have not appeared, stop here. Record "style payload visible, build conditions have not appeared." Do not write this up as a conclusion about lock or license, or hand off the same observation as an exit action.

**The relationship can now be tied to the current chain**

Check the exit action. If the old relationship is the one to withdraw, first confirm which relationship the page still displays, then perform the withdrawal; afterward, check only whether the old edge has disappeared. If the old edge is still there, retain that result and stop. Do not substitute repeated withdrawals for assessment.

**The entry point remains, but the explanatory text cannot be traced back**

Keep the current entry point and remove the explanatory text that cannot be traced back. Do not add a speculative source explanation here. If the original record becomes available later, re-enter the tree from that record.

**The symptom concerns permissions rather than the relationship itself**

Record which detail page or action entry point is restricted and hand it over to the owner of those permissions. Include only the first failing sample, the minimal reproduction, and the branch reached in the handoff; if the long-term maintainer is unknown, do not fill one in here.

## Stop Conditions

Stop making further inferences if any of the following occurs:

- There is no minimal reproduction;
- The style payload is visible but the build conditions are missing;
- The current chain cannot be distinguished from the old relationship;
- A restricted detail page must be viewed to continue.

When stopping, clearly record the observations so far and the missing item. The recovery action has not yet been tried in a shared environment; until a usable environment is available, do not treat the withdrawal result as an established fact.

# Package Release On-Call FAQ

Three questions recur in the on-call records. They concern what the entry point can confirm, where responsibility lies when withdrawing candidate paths, and when the card can be closed. The early answers remain in the records, but they must not be merged with the later review into a single statement.

## What can the existing declaration-surface entry point prove?

It can be used to check the public declaration surface and whether the candidate path actually points to this entry point. An early answer said, "finding the entry point is enough." That statement is retained in the old guidance; after the actual review, it can only serve as confirmation at the entry-point level. It cannot by itself prove that the release succeeded, adjacent regression tests have been completed, or withdrawal coverage is in place.

During on-call shifts, it's easy to record "the declaration can be found" and "it can be withdrawn" as the same thing. The former is a local check through the entry point; the latter still requires someone to record the trade-offs for the candidate path and depends on the rollback arrangements left in place for the release window. If only one new error has been added in the meantime, with no adjacent regression results, the record remains in candidate status.

## Who is responsible for withdrawing candidate paths?

The old answer simply said, "the package release on-call is responsible." This identifies where the on-call role picks things up; it does not mean the on-call can make the call for all candidate paths. When withdrawal is involved, there must be a record of the owner's trade-offs. If all that has been found is the relationship between an entry point and a candidate path, and no one has confirmed the withdrawal, there is still no clear ownership for the issue. Don't substitute finding the entry point for confirmation of responsibility.

The question about the browser realm trace can be logged, but there is no answer here. It should not be recorded as evidence that an owner has already confirmed it, nor does it replace the review of the entry point and adjacent regressions.

## Under what conditions can it be closed?

The old draft said, "close once the entry-point review passes and there are no new errors." This statement is retained in the old version. The closure rule now used by the on-call is: a card can be closed only after the target entry point and adjacent regression tests have both been rerun, the owner has recorded the trade-offs, and rollback coverage has been confirmed for the release window.

versions.body:
# Freeze Window Decision Record

This freeze discussion could initially have been framed too easily as a question of whether to keep or remove a component-meta entry point. What it actually needed to address was something else: under what evidence conditions the compatibility train can stop expanding, and which consumer cases still have to remain outside the window. The entry point is only the most visible location in this process; changing it directly would instead disguise an unverified scope as a completed switch.

This record retains the original conclusion: this round will not adjust the freeze window to chase more scope, will retain the current component-meta entry point, and will approve only the portion covered by existing evidence. Here, "retain" does not declare the old entry point the long-term default, nor does it let all subsequent changes continue to pile up there. It means that during the freeze there is still a reversible old path, so confirmed consumer samples do not lose a landing point because of the window discussion.

There were two approaches on the table.

The first was to maintain the current entry point and set the freeze boundary around samples that could already be rerun. The cost was direct: some cases that people hoped to close out with the train would have to keep waiting, and the window would not appear larger simply because one round received a green signal. But this path did not require unknown cases to be classified as compatible in advance, and it left consumers a place to review through the existing entry point.

The second was to adjust the window and treat the current pass signal as grounds for expanding the freeze scope. Its appeal was that the handoff would be cleaner, with the entry point and window apparently folded into the same round of changes. The review did not adopt it. The issue was not the act of "adjusting" itself, but that it would require us to answer a question that had not yet been answered: after the adjustment, would behavior across the compiler-chain and runtime boundaries still be represented by the same set of samples? The meeting did not replace that question with a more appealing assumption.

The compatibility train is based on consumer Fang Ke observed behavior and rerunnable samples; a single green signal cannot replace checking across the compiler-chain and runtime boundaries. This is the decision criterion for this trade-off, not an additional formal gate. A passing result on the compiler side can only say something about the objects covered by that result; when the runtime side has not been observed under the same conditions, the latter conclusion cannot be inferred from the former. Conversely, a consumer that is temporarily not in the sample set should not be recorded as a failure. It simply has not yet entered this round's approved scope.

Accordingly, the freeze window uses "evidence-based approval," not "entry-state-based approval." The current component-meta entry point remains; that does not mean all related paths can be released. If the entry point is replaced later, that cannot be used to conclude that the earlier samples were invalid. Entry-point state and compatibility judgment must be recorded separately here. The former concerns a reversible operating point; the latter concerns what the train can actually commit to.

This distinction also explains why the window-adjustment approach was not recorded as a tentative decision. If the window is changed first and samples are filled in later, consumers see a scope signal first and only learn afterward how much of it has actually been rerun. If the approved scope is pinned to the samples first, the window is conservative, but the coordination cost is not shifted to whoever takes over later. During the freeze, the latter is closer to the actual impact: observed behavior can continue with the train; unobserved behavior does not automatically receive the same conclusion because the name is similar or the entry point is the same.

Retaining the old entry point also has a narrower meaning. It should be reversible, not a parallel channel with no exit condition. The review did not approve a specific withdrawal point, and withdrawal was not written as a deliverable for the current round. What can be established now is that if this entry point is changed later, the record must show the scope approved at that time and which consumer samples were not included in that approval. Otherwise, the withdrawal action will be conflated with the freeze judgment, making it impossible afterward to explain what the rollback targeted or which scope had never been put on the train.

The meeting materials required the actual impact, a coordinator, and a reversible old entry point to be recorded. The actual impact has been recorded by approved scope: consumer behavior covered by existing evidence can enter the freeze judgment; the uncovered portion does not expand along with the window. For coordination, the quality side retains the entry point for the freeze judgment, while the integration side is responsible for bringing the rerun status of consumer samples back to the discussion. Both sides need to speak to the same sample scope, rather than each using a single pass record to stand in for the other side's check. No separate role was defined for "having one person close all issues," because window judgment and consumer coordination are two different kinds of work to begin with.

During the review, the wording of this decision was revisited as well. The original "retain the entry point" could easily be read as "the entry point has been confirmed risk-free," so this version spells out the distinction: the entry point is retained to give the known scope a reversible location; approval is still determined by consumer Fang Ke observed behavior and rerunnable samples. The original conservative conclusion has not been withdrawn. The review also did not upgrade a single green signal into cross-boundary proof.

The relationship for this round can be simplified as the flow below. It is not an execution sequence diagram; it explains why the approved scope cannot be inferred directly from an entry point or a passing result:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Consumer Fang Ke observed behavior] --> B[Rerunnable samples]
  B --> C{Covered across compiler-chain and runtime boundaries}
  C -->|Yes| D[Approve corresponding scope]
  C -->|No| E[Do not expand the freeze scope]
  D --> F[Retain the current component-meta entry point]
  E --> F
```

The "do not expand" in the diagram does not mean stopping the investigation, nor does it mean labeling uncovered objects negatively. It is only how the freeze window is handled: objects without enough material this round are not moved into the already approved scope. This leaves uneven edges, but it is easier to review later than to clean those edges up into a seemingly complete compatibility line.

The detailed handoff for the browser-matrix switch is recorded separately in DOC-52. That handoff can help determine where sample maintenance goes, but it does not change the window decision in this record: organizing the browser matrix does not automatically constitute evidence that the compiler-chain and runtime boundaries have been covered.

What remains unresolved is still the samples themselves, not the wording. What needs to be clarified is which consumer samples are already rerunnable, which compiler chains and runtime boundaries they each pass through, and which side will confirm a scope change before the old entry point is withdrawn. Until those facts are added, do not describe the result of this round as "the window has been adjusted."
